detail.abstract: The 21st century, marked by the era of electronic evolution, has revolutionized our lives, enhancing our independence and broadening our access to advanced techniques and technologies. E-evolution, a digital transition process, intertwines social development with cyberspace communication, systematization, virtual and augmented reality, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, machine learning, and big data. In the modern information society, we are confronted with a surge in the negative impact of entirely new factors. Cyber war, cyber attack, information war, color revolution, trolling, astroturfing, fake news, and information are not just buzzwords but serious threats that significantly alter the theory and practice of security. Our ability to mitigate and resist these threats is being tested, making fortifying our defenses and minimizing damage a pressing concern for the social security of nations. Protecting our society's material and spiritual values, maintaining law and order, ensuring social stability based on the principle of social justice, and strengthening national unity are not just ideals but the very foundation of our social security. The urgency of this task cannot be overstated.

title: Is There Economics in Vampirism? Incentives, Asymmetry and Opportunism

detail.title: Is There Economics in Vampirism? Incentives, Asymmetry and Opportunism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No new data were generated or analyzed in support of this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or animals, and therefore ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this study

detail.abstract: This paper develops a principal-agent model to study asymmetric cooperation in which an opportunistic agent appropriates the surplus generated by a principal's effort. We call this configuration economic vampirism. The baseline environment features linear technology and quadratic effort costs. Without enforceable sharing, the agent sets φ = 0, the principal's optimal effort collapses to e * P = 0, and output falls. We introduce a psychological amplifier, ressentiment (Nietzsche, 1887), captured by a parameter ρ ≥ 0 in the agent's payoff. Higher ρ strengthens hostility toward recognition and further depresses feasible sharing under reputation or contracts. Comparative statics show a declining sustainability locus φ R (ρ) and the induced leftward shift on e * P (φ), tightening cooperative equilibria. The model explains non-convex cost patterns and multiple efficient scales, clarifying how coordination, reputation, and incentive design interact with psychosocial drivers. Applications to academia, electoral politics, and Inconfidência Mineira illustrate the mechanism. Policy implications include contractual recognition, clawback clauses, and reputational enforcement to deter opportunism and preserve cooperation.

title: Assessing the Impact of Digital Technologies on the Taxation of the Informal Economy in Nigeria
affiliations: UNIVERSITY OF BENIN, BENIN CITY , FACULTY OF MANAGEMENT SCIENCE

detail.title: Assessing the Impact of Digital Technologies on the Taxation of the Informal Economy in Nigeria
detail.abstract:
The informal economy plays a significant role in Nigeria's socioeconomic landscape, yet it often operates outside the purview of formal taxation. This research project aims to assess the transformative impact of digital technologies on the taxation of the informal economy in Nigeria.

With the rapid proliferation of digital technologies, including mobile payment systems, e-commerce platforms, digital identity system, the internet, this study investigatedhow these innovations have influenced tax compliance, revenue collection, and regulatory efforts within the informal sector. By employing a combination of qualitative and quantitative research methods, including surveys, interviews, and data analysis such as regression analysis and ANOVA test, this project seeks to provide insights into the changing dynamics of taxation in the informal economy.

Key objectives include to identify the potential of digital technologies, such as mobile phones, electronic invoicing, and digital identity systems, in enhancing tax collection and administration in the informal economy, to examine the current state of digital technology adoption and utilization in the taxation of the informal economy in Nigeria, to identify the challenges and opportunities associated with implementing digital technologies in the taxation of the informal economy, to examine the impact of digital technologies in the tax compliance behaviour of informal economy participants in Nigeria.

The findings of this research are expected to shed light on the potentials, current state of digital technologies,opportunities and challenges associated with incorporating digital technologies into the taxation of the informal economy and its impact on the taxation of the informal economy in Nigeria. Ultimately, the study aims to offer valuable recommendations to policymakers, tax authorities, and stakeholders, with the goal of enhancing tax compliance, promoting economic inclusivity, and fostering sustainable growth in this crucial sector of the Nigerian economy.

title: Right, Left, and the Algorithm: An Experimental Audit of Political Exposure on TikTok

detail.title: Right, Left, and the Algorithm: An Experimental Audit of Political Exposure on TikTok

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
TikTok is currently the fastest-growing social media platform worldwide, with over 1.6 billion active monthly users, most of whom belong to the Generation Z. Its success is driven by a highly personalised recommender system that curates each user’s "For You Page". Designed to maximise engagement, this algorithm not only reflects user interests but can also shape their views and priorities by repeatedly exposing them to certain types of content. Despite its societal impact, little empirical work has examined how TikTok’s recommender system can amplify ideological content in differential ways, and how user engagement shapes these recommendation patterns. 

This thesis addresses this gap through an experimental audit using three sock-puppet accounts engaging with right-aligned, left-aligned, or no political content. Based on a dataset of 1,200 recommended videos, the findings reveal that right-aligned engagement rapidly produces highly saturated filter bubbles dominated by conspiratorial, nationalist, and exclusionary narratives, alongside emotionally charged framings such as fear appeals and outrage. In contrast, left-aligned engagement leads to a slower and less complete filter bubble formation, with feeds remaining more moderate and including diverse or even oppositional content. These results demonstrate that TikTok’s recommender system shapes political information environments asymmetrically, with potential implications for ideological polarisation and public discourse among young users.

title: Green HR: Empowering Circular Economies through People and Processes
affiliations: , Vidya Jyothi Institute of Technology, KSRM COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING (Autonomous) and Bengaluru City University

detail.title: Green HR: Empowering Circular Economies through People and Processes
detail.abstract:
Today, sustainability is the core constituent of organisations aiming to achieve long-term success in this 
fast-changing business world. CEM is a practical method of waste minimization and maximum use of 
resources. The role of HR in CEM is to create a culture of teamwork and continuous improvement among 
employees in delivering Customer Experience Management. There are certain changes that occur in the 
basis of change attractiveness and retention capacity on the one hand and decreases negative impacts on 
the environment, and so this calls for the implementation of Green HR practices. A major study 
comprising 276 participants affirms the strong link between the performance of CEM and Green HR 
practices promoting people-oriented initiatives toward sustainable growth. Results of this study offer 
practical guidance for firms wishing to harness their human resources toward making them 
environmentally friendly to heighten their efficiency in operations.

title: What's Pulse Like, the Orlando Gay Club where the Worst Massacre in U.S. History Occurred?

detail.title: What's Pulse Like, the Orlando Gay Club where the Worst Massacre in U.S. History Occurred?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This article was written under the will of informing the community
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article doesn't include any patient information or study
declarations.funderStatement: This article received no financing from external sources

detail.abstract: This article portrays Pulse, a popular gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida, that became the site of the deadliest mass shooting in U.S. history on June 12, 2016. Through testimonies and vivid descriptions, it recounts Pulse’s vibrant atmosphere, its themed nights, and its significance as a cultural hub for the city’s LGBTQ+ and Latino communities. Once a safe and emblematic space for entertainment, diversity, and artistic expression, Pulse transformed overnight into a place of mourning after an armed attacker killed 49 people and injured dozens more. The narrative situates Pulse not only as a nightclub but also as a symbol of inclusion and community resilience in the face of tragedy.

title: The normative value of a revised choice: a structural approach
affiliations: The University of Toledo, Department of Economics

detail.title: The normative value of a revised choice: a structural approach
detail.abstract: When participants in an economic experiment are given an opportunity to revise their choices, this is often interpreted as revising a mistake. I assess the normative value of revised choice using structural modeling. Participants' revisions are mostly to choices that yield greater utility. However a substantial minority of participants experience a utility loss on average as a result of their revisions.

title: Success factors for young science and technology parks.
affiliations: Kingston University - School of Computer Science and Mathematics, Zayed University and Kingston University

detail.title: Success factors for young science and technology parks.
detail.abstract: This paper presents some novel-seeming concepts derived from new data-driven approaches. An overview of studies on the organic growth of young start-up Science and Technology Parks (STP), using Big Data, econometric analyses, panel data and computer simulations is presented. Results and concepts derived from industrialised countries, notably Sweden and the UK, may well be applicable to some emerging economies. Results are of interest to technology entrepreneurs considering choosing a STP to inhabit, as well as those in the central team, specialising in management and enterprise development, including growing new Parks.

title: Diluting Exclusivity? The Prevalence and Distribution of Bursaries and Scholarships for Britain's Private Schools
affiliations: University College London - UCL Institute of Education, University College London - UCL Institute of Education, University of Warwick and University College London

detail.title: Diluting Exclusivity? The Prevalence and Distribution of Bursaries and Scholarships for Britain's Private Schools
detail.abstract: Bursaries and scholarships are sometimes advanced as a mitigating factor for Britain's private schools' social exclusiveness and as a vehicle for social reform. This paper analyses trends in these grants since 1997 using the Family Resources Survey. We find that one in ten private school pupils received a bursary or scholarship, while only 3.4 percent of total fees were mitigated in this way. Over time the grants became more common but decreased in value relative to fees. Across income groups, grants were partly progressive, but became less so over time. Across occupational classes, grant frequency was consistently neutral, but grant amounts were somewhat progressive. Drawing on these findings and on historical evidence from the 20 th century, the paper concludes that bursaries and scholarships are unlikely to bring forth a significant reform of the socioeconomic sectoral divide in Britain's school system.

title: Tariff Communication and the Repricing of U.S. Sovereign Risk
affiliations: Linkoping University

detail.title: Tariff Communication and the Repricing of U.S. Sovereign Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the high-frequency impact of President Donald J. Trump's social media communications regarding tariffs and trade policy on U.S. bond markets. Using a unique dataset of 45 tariff-related announcements from the first 100 days of the second Trump administration, this study employs a local projections methodology on 5-minute data for U.S. Treasury yields, equity prices, and exchange rates to estimate the dynamic effects of these events. Tariff and trade-related announcements are found to trigger a statistically and economically significant increase in U.S. Treasury yields across the yield curve, with nominal yields rising by 4-8 basis points over a multi-day horizon. The results show that the increase in yields is almost entirely driven by an increase in real yields, while market-based measures of inflation expectations remain stable. This evidence suggests that the primary transmission channel is an increase in the real risk premium demanded by investors due to heightened policy uncertainty, rather than a revision of inflation expectations. These findings demonstrate that modern political communication can serve as a significant risk factor, directly increasing the real cost of government borrowing.

title:
THE CRITICAL ROLE OF CONVENTIONAL BELIEFS IN ECONOMICS: MULTIPLE 
𝒓*'s AND STRUCTURAL INDETERMINACIES

detail.title:
THE CRITICAL ROLE OF CONVENTIONAL BELIEFS IN ECONOMICS: MULTIPLE 
𝒓*'s AND STRUCTURAL INDETERMINACIES
detail.abstract: This article examines how conventional beliefs influence the natural interest rate (𝑟*). The article argues that 𝑟* is not pinned down by fundamentals but a belief-contingent variable influenced by prevailing expectations. When agents hold pessimistic views about future demand or policy effectiveness, the economy may settle into low-growth, low-rate equilibria; conversely, optimistic beliefs can lead to higher growth rates. This belief-driven behavior creates multiple equilibria, endogenous liquidity traps, and hysteresis, regardless of structural frictions. Traditional methods struggle to identify 𝑟* accurately across different regimes, resulting in policy miscalibration. The existence of multiple belief-consistent natural rates introduces policy multiplicity, where rules effective in one belief regime may conflict in another. These findings challenge the structural view of 𝑟* and suggest a need for credibility-sensitive policy frameworks to manage expectations effectively.

title: Expected Utility Loss in Mean-Variance Portfolios with Transaction Costs
affiliations: University of Agder - School of Business and Law

detail.title: Expected Utility Loss in Mean-Variance Portfolios with Transaction Costs
detail.abstract: We extend the analytical framework of Kan and Zhou (2007) for evaluating the expected out-of-sample utility loss from parameter uncertainty in mean-variance (MV) portfolio selection by incorporating proportional transaction costs. Focusing on the tractable case of known covariance and unknown mean excess returns, we derive closed-form expressions quantifying how trading frictions interact with estimation risk to reduce portfolio performance. The analysis yields simple formulas for the critical estimation window length at which the expected utility of the sample-based MV strategy equals that of the equally-weighted (1/N) portfolio, both with and without transaction costs. An empirical illustration using U.S. equity portfolios shows that even modest proportional costs can substantially increase the required sample size, in some cases to impractical levels. The results highlight the importance of accounting for trading frictions when assessing the implementability of mean-variance optimization in finite samples.

title: From Savings Push to Demand Pull: Dynamic Consumption Externalities and Optimal Industrial Upgrading
affiliations: University of Hong Kong (HKU), HKU Business School and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-Shenzhen)

detail.title: From Savings Push to Demand Pull: Dynamic Consumption Externalities and Optimal Industrial Upgrading
detail.abstract: We develop a tractable macro-development model to study industrial upgrading in catching-up economies. The model incorporates hierarchical demand in preferences and learning-by-doing in production into a two-sector growth framework. It captures a dynamic feedback loop: income growth expands consumption frontiers (income-push), while demand for advanced goods drives technological progress (demand-pull). The laissez-faire equilibrium exhibits two-sided inefficiencies due to dynamic production externalities---excessive early-stage consumption delays capital accumulation, whereas insufficient later-stage consumption limits productivity spillovers. Optimal policy entails a two-phase intervention: initially suppressing consumption to prioritize investment, followed by stimulating consumption to exploit spillovers. Targeted industrial policies facilitate the timely rebalancing toward consumption-led growth, averting productivity traps. Empirical evidence and quantitative analysis support the model.

title: Asset Pricing under Inferential Complexity
affiliations: Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School

detail.title: Asset Pricing under Inferential Complexity
detail.abstract: I develop a continuous-time general equilibrium model in which heterogeneous investors allocate wealth across assets that differ in inferential complexity, defined as the epistemic difficulty of learning latent asset characteristics through noisy signals. Investors update beliefs via Bayesian learning but face persistent disutility from inferential frictions. Complexity enters preferences as an endogenous utility penalty tied to posterior uncertainty and belief dispersion. The resulting pricing kernel yields a closed-form decomposition of expected returns into standard risk premia and a distinct complexity premium.

title: Beyond Iusmorphs: Advanced Evolutionary Models for Legal Systems

detail.title: Beyond Iusmorphs: Advanced Evolutionary Models for Legal Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest declared. This research was conducted independently without commercial interests or financial relationships that could influence the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This computational research does not involve human participants or patient data. Analysis uses only publicly available legal reform data from published sources.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received. This research was self-funded by the author.

keywords: Reality Filter JEL Classification: K00 (Law and Economics

detail.abstract:
This paper documents the evolution from Iusmorphs V5.0 (random walk exploration in IuSpace) to V6.0 (structured evolutionary simulation), implementing three advanced evolutionary models inspired by Richard Dawkins' post-Biomorphs work: Caparazomorfos (parametric exploration), Artromorfos (embryological construction), and NetSpinner (population dynamics with gene flow). 
While V5.0 established robust empirical validation (87.4% accuracy predicting implementation gaps across 18 global reforms, 2015-2024), it lacked the evolutionary simulation mechanisms required to model legal norm evolution dynamically. V6.0 completes this architecture by adding genetic representation, evolutionary operators, and genealogy tracking, while integrating with existing validated infrastructure (legal-memespace, RootFinder). 
The unified framework offers four exploration modes optimized for different use cases: EMERGENT (discovery through serendipity), PARAMETRIC (systematic comparison), EMBRYOLOGICAL (document generation with structural guarantees), and POPULATION (comparative law with legal transplants modeling). 
Preliminary validation (n=3, underpowered at 15% statistical power) shows simulated gene flow rate (33%) trending toward documented base rate (45%) but with wide confidence intervals [0.8%, 90.6%] precluding robust inference. We propose staged validation roadmap requiring 85-244 events for statistical confirmation. 
This work provides proof-of-concept that evolutionary computation can provide powerful analytical tools for understanding legal systems evolution, institutional convergence, and legal transplants dynamics.

title: Does Ideological Polarization Lead to Policy Polarization? *
affiliations: Charles III University of Madrid

detail.title: Does Ideological Polarization Lead to Policy Polarization? *
detail.abstract: I study an election between two ideologically polarized parties that are both office-and policymotivated. The parties compete by proposing policies on a single issue. The analysis uncovers a non-monotonic relationship between ideological and policy polarization. When ideological polarization is low, an increase leads to policy moderation; when it is high, the opposite occurs, and policies become more extreme. Moreover, incorporating ideological polarization refines our understanding of the role of valence: both high-and low-valence candidates may adopt more extreme positions, depending on the electorate's degree of ideological polarization.

title: Inflation Expectations and a Conservative Central Banker: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank and University of Giessen

detail.title: Inflation Expectations and a Conservative Central Banker: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
detail.abstract: This paper studies the response of inflation expectations to an exogenous shift in central bank preferences. We use the unexpected announcement of the resignation of Jens Weidmann, the president of the Deutsche Bundesbank, in 2021 as a natural experiment constituting a rare case of an exogenous shift in the composition of the ECB's Governing Council. As a member of the Governing Council, he was a known policy hawk and a vocal critic of the ECB's asset purchases. Our evidence from survey data suggests that the news about the resignation causes a strong increase in individual inflation uncertainty of German households and a significant fall in the level of trust in the ECB. The effect on the mean inflation expectations remains inconclusive. Thus, the shift in policy preferences has a strong effect on second moments, while the first moment effect remains weak.

title: All Enterprise Must Go into the Hands of the Central Bank, Eventually: Arson
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh

detail.title: All Enterprise Must Go into the Hands of the Central Bank, Eventually: Arson
detail.abstract: A reputable British university inexplicably features an integrated 'Business Gateway' on its campus. British Business Gateways lend a hand with the formation of new companies, or 'start-ups.' The mystery deepens, as all of the afore-mentioned university's business students are required to present business plans of hypothetical start-ups. Eventual oral examinations on the universal business ideas inexplicably all theme the formation of new restaurants. Continue the puzzle, search for the brick-and-mortar facilities of the university's selfadvertised medical unit, and you'll be unsuccessful. There are no medicine students. The university is a concealed food and drug administration, a public yet secret institution that checks on food quality. Yes, the university has medical equipment but it's not for medical use but for food inspection. Meanwhile, if you search Britain for jobs in the private industry, you'll end up with the real rotten tomatoes. So far, morally speaking, that's all fine. Organising your economy upside-down is not a crime. Secrecy is not a crime. The secrecy around food hygiene might in fact be necessitated. The real-life scenario dips hopelessly unacceptable when that same country forces its job seekers to apply at its leftto-rot fringe of private industry. While you don't care one bit, let me unwind the truth, suspicious-ownership Britain.

title: How Firms Recover after Floods: Mechanisms and Evidence

detail.title: How Firms Recover after Floods: Mechanisms and Evidence
detail.abstract: Floods are among the costliest natural disasters, yet we know little about what drives business recovery. This gap matters as the incidence of flooding increases and government bailouts may become more limited under tightening fiscal budgets. Using establishment-level data that link remote sensing inundation to FEMA flood maps, I provide novel causal evidence that flood insurance is a key driver of business recovery. I combine a triple difference design around Hurricane Sandy with a spatial regression discontinuity at floodplain borders. Flooded establishments just inside floodplains, where properties with federally backed or regulated mortgages must carry flood insurance, recover more in employment and sales than otherwise similar sites just outside. Effects are larger where firms are more likely to be insured and where policy limits can cover more losses. Establishments of firms that disclosed insurance pre-flood also recover more. These patterns reflect an insurance-liquidity channel that supports rebuilding and reallocation, allowing firms to return stronger rather than merely to baseline. In equity markets, price drops around flood news are smaller for firms with prior exposure or disclosure. Overall, the evidence indicates insurance coverage materially shapes business recovery.

title: From Extraction to Inference: Comparing Rule-Based, Machine Learning, and LLM Approaches for Classifying Social Outcomes in Legal Text
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Sociology, Yale University, The Chinese University of Hong Kong and Brown University

detail.title: From Extraction to Inference: Comparing Rule-Based, Machine Learning, and LLM Approaches for Classifying Social Outcomes in Legal Text
detail.abstract: Legal texts encode key social outcomes, but their unstructured format, domain-specific language, and culturally embedded cues make them difficult to analyze computationally. This study compares five classification approaches: rule-based extraction, traditional supervised machine learning (SML), fine-tuned encoder models, fine-tuned decoder large language models (LLMs), and zero-shot decoder LLMs, on 3,602 Chinese divorce judgments. We evaluate performance across three classification tasks that vary in linguistic regularity, contextual ambiguity, and cultural embeddedness: litigant gender, child custody rulings, and housing property outcomes. Our findings show that no single method is universally optimal; while rule-based and traditional models perform well on routine legal outcomes, fine-tuned decoder LLMs, especially the closed-source, commercial model GPT-4o-mini, achieve the most consistent and accurate performance for tasks requiring inference from implicit or socially embedded cues. We analyze typologies of human–machine disagreement and demonstrate that LLMs can identify annotation oversights and remain robust to small or noisy training sets. Building on these insights, we introduce a Task-Aware Diagnostic Framework that connects textual complexity to methodological choice, offering a systematic guide for sociologists using LLMs to extract and infer social outcomes from institutional text.

title: Virtual person in the realm of profiling practices: Who is profiling Who? Who is profiled in the end?
affiliations: KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP), KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP) and KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP)

detail.title: Virtual person in the realm of profiling practices: Who is profiling Who? Who is profiled in the end?
detail.abstract: Big Data Analytics has become increasingly important in both private and public sectors due to its significant economic and commercial advantages. Data is now an integral asset in a data-driven economy, pivotal in decision-making processes and business launchings. The collection and analysis of vast amounts of data are directed towards comprehending future behaviours, specifically on profiling data subjects. This paper focuses on the complex processes of collecting and analysing extensive datasets through Big Data Analytics, particularly emphasising the profiling practice. Primarily focusing on the European Union (EU) legal framework, the concept of profiling is examined through a nuanced and multifaceted perspective encompassing both legal and technological dimensions. Additionally, the paper introduces and explores the concept of a virtual person, which serves as a veil to conceal the identity of the data subjects in the context of profiling practices. Hence, this paper examines profiling practices based on data derived from virtual persons concerning the accuracy principle outlined in the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Lastly, the paper emphasises the pivotal role of electronic identification in shaping profiling practices by clarifying the evolving distinctions between virtual and natural persons.

title: Employer Monopsony Power Does Not Reduce the Value of a Statistical Life
affiliations: Vanderbilt University, Law School, Law and Economics, Students, Claremont Graduate University - Department of Economic Sciences and Vanderbilt University - Law School

detail.title: Employer Monopsony Power Does Not Reduce the Value of a Statistical Life
detail.abstract: Although wage rates are lower when employers have monopsony power, we find that the value of a statistical life (VSL) is not reduced when labor markets are more concentrated. Because the estimated VSL is the product of the wage and the wage-risk tradeoff rate, a greater tradeoff rate in highly concentrated U.S. labor markets produces a larger VSL. The general relationship we find is robust with respect to different labor market data. Our results provide the first evidence contradicting policy-related concerns that the VSL is lower in monopsonistic labor markets.

title: Is Suboptimality Safe in the Age of AI?
affiliations: Independent, University of East Anglia (UEA) - Centre for Behavioural and Experimental Social Science (CBESS) and University of East Anglia (UEA) - School of Economics

detail.title: Is Suboptimality Safe in the Age of AI?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All participants in this study were anonymous.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the researchers themselves.

detail.abstract:
Social reform has historically been proposed and led by humans, but we may wonder if some future social reforms could be proposed or led by AI. If negligence is blameworthy, then AI might even deserve blame if it never serves as our moral and social leader (or we might deserve blame for never producing AI that should serve in that way). 

As a concrete and measurable example of where AI could lead us to treat each other better, this paper offers a game-theoretic examination of a common resource-division problem. Study 1 reports recent results of behavioural economics experiments with this multi-player game. The human behaviour observed in the study is so far from optimal as to imply that ceding some autonomy to AI-or at least some leadership to AI-might be in our best interest. Rather than mitigate the social harms associated with caste systems (such as racism, sexism, etc), the anonymity of the online game setting appears to simply reallocate harm less systematically. Thus, to actually cure some of our most pressing modern social problems may even require guidance by some form of AI. Standard open-source oTree software to reproduce these results is made available on GitHub. 

Study 2 involves philosophical thought experiments in the style of Nozick's "Experience machine". To facilitate discussion about when suboptimality might qualify as "safe" generally, an evidence-based leadership-sharing framework aligning with the Scientist AI approach of LawZero and Yoshua Bengio is conceptualized to ask when one might preserve the opportunity to make mistakes (i.e., to not use the hypothetically perfect machine). Would we extend the same privilege to AI? While Study 1 offers evidence to support the Scientist AI approach for some contexts, we believe Study 2 justifies urgency for a deeper discussion about the pursuit of optimality and its consequences for our own autonomy.

title: Legal and Ethical Implications of Biometric Data Collection in Ghana: A Study of the Ghana Card under the National Identification System
affiliations: Public Relations Ghana

detail.title: Legal and Ethical Implications of Biometric Data Collection in Ghana: A Study of the Ghana Card under the National Identification System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: In 2019, Ghana relaunched the National Identification Authority's (NIA) Ghana Card project, with over 18 million citizens reportedly enrolled as of September 30, 2025. The initiative required collecting and storing extensive personal and biometric data, including full names, nationality, marital status, occupation, fingerprints, facial images, and iris scans. The government justified the project as a tool to combat cybercrime, improve policy design, and drive Ghana's digitisation agenda. While it promises national security and governance benefits, the exercise also raises serious legal and ethical concerns about privacy, surveillance, data protection, and potential misuse. This study employs doctrinal research to evaluate the adequacy of Ghana's legal framework and ethical standards in safeguarding biometric data, complemented by a socio-legal approach to identify regulatory and enforcement gaps. It benchmarks Ghana's practices against international norms, conventions, and human rights standards. Ultimately, the paper proposes reforms to strengthen protections, contribute to scholarship, raise awareness about privacy breaches, and advance African digital rights debates.

title: Designing a Predictable Retirement Income under the National Pension System
affiliations: Samasthiti Advisors

detail.title: Designing a Predictable Retirement Income under the National Pension System
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates PFRDA (2025) proposals for enhancing the National Pension System (NPS). Using stochastic simulations based on Indian return and inflation data, the study assesses the sustainability and design efficacy of two key prototype schemes-the Step-Up Systematic Withdrawal plus Annuity Hybrid (Pension Scheme 1) and the Assured Inflation-Linked Pension (Pension Scheme 2). Results indicate that Scheme 1, with a 35% equity allocation and a 4.5% initial withdrawal rate stepped up by 0.25% annually, yields required annuity rates of roughly 3.4-6.8%, well within prevailing market pricing. The design offers behavioural simplicity with limited investment or pricing risk, though purchasing-power erosion post-annuitization remains a concern. Scheme 2 achieves a highly predictable, inflation-indexed income stream with negligible failure probability. Its dual-pool structure-combining a risk-free base and a growth buffer-transforms retirement savings into a real-value pension. The embedded 3.5% withdrawal rate aligns closely with sustainable withdrawal estimates from prior Indian studies. Overall, the consultation paper's framework represents a timely and positive evolution of India's pension policy, from accumulation-focused savings to outcome oriented retirement income. This paper is part of an ongoing research effort on retirement-income design under India's National Pension System. It is circulated as a working paper to invite feedback.

title: Organizational Persons, Business Firms, and Market Institutions
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Legal Studies and Business Ethics Department

detail.title: Organizational Persons, Business Firms, and Market Institutions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: No additional funding beyond university research support.

detail.abstract: This chapter presents an overview of the nature of social organizations and institutions with a specific focus on business firms and economic markets. Business organizations and market institutions are generally understood as aiming to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of the production of goods, services, and information-and to channel and condition their distribution. In the words of Thomas Hobbes, they should enable "commodious living." In their operations, however, they can also pose challenges to the underlying sustainability of the natural and social systems on which they rely. An understanding of the nature of business firms and market institutions-that is, their ontology-is helpful to counter their potential for causing trouble and harm, departing from their original social purposes. In other words, we need to understand business firms operating in markets because they can become, like Frankenstein's monster, unmoored from the reasons for their creation. This chapter is therefore not only descriptive but prescriptive. An understanding of the social ontology of business firms and market institutions is a prerequisite for recommending how to change them when needed. An additional thesis is that reform is needed today.

title: Mitigating Overfitting in Hyperparameter Selection for Trading Strategies Using Randomized In-Sample Evaluation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Mitigating Overfitting in Hyperparameter Selection for Trading Strategies Using Randomized In-Sample Evaluation
detail.abstract: In quantitative finance and algorithmic trading, hyperparameter tuning is often performed via a traditional train-test split, with the best-performing model on the in-sample data evaluated on a holdout set. However, this approach is prone to overfitting, particularly when evaluating a large grid of parameters, as it optimizes to a single realization of the in-sample period. In this study, we propose a robust method to reduce overfitting by introducing randomized subsampling within the in-sample (training) data. Instead of selecting hyperparameters based solely on performance over a single in-sample period, we compute pooled Sharpe ratios from multiple random samples of the training set. The hyperparameters with the highest pooled Sharpe ratio are then tested on the out-of-sample data. We empirically compare this method to the classic approach across a large grid of strategy parameters. Using statistical testing on the ranks of parameter performance, we show that our method yields lower rank divergence between in-sample and out-of-sample performance, indicating a more stable and less overfit model selection process. This framework offers a practical enhancement to hyperparameter selection workflows in trading strategy development.

title: Why Insurers Price Carbon Low: An Analysis of Financed Emissions and Investment Decisions
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business and

detail.title: Why Insurers Price Carbon Low: An Analysis of Financed Emissions and Investment Decisions
detail.abstract: Recent research by McKinsey & Company finds that the insurance sector has the lowest median internal carbon price (ICP) across thirteen sectors. In this paper, we rationalize the low ICP through an analysis of insurers' emissions, which are predominately financed emissions. We develop and analytically solve an extended mean-variance model with a constraint on portfolio emissions. Our model identifies an emission-efficient frontier (EEF) for environmentally conscious investors. We use the EEF to analyze the expected impact of an internal carbon policy and show that the policy is most effective when brown assets yield only modest performance. Using emissions data from London Stock Exchange Group, we empirically estimate the EEF. According to our model, to maximize the insurer's carbon-adjusted Sharpe ratio, the ICP should not exceed $4.7 per tonne. Meanwhile, the estimated expected policy impact is high, and hence even a low ICP can reduce insurers' financed emissions substantially with little compromise in investment performance. Our findings support the use of low ICPs for financed emissions. Moreover, we question the practices of benchmarking ICPs across all scopes against recommended ranges by leading international climate bodies and applying uniform carbon pricing throughout an organization.

title: Borrowing Size and Functions from Nearby Cities: The Mediating Role of Inter-Municipal Cooperation
affiliations: Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique (INRA) - CESAER, Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique (INRA) - CESAER and Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique (INRA) - CESAER

detail.title: Borrowing Size and Functions from Nearby Cities: The Mediating Role of Inter-Municipal Cooperation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report no potential conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics are needed as public data.

detail.abstract: This paper first analyzes whether efficiency gains coming from agglomeration effects in larger municipalities can benefit their smaller neighbors through 'borrowed size' and 'borrowed functions' mechanisms, and second, it explores the role of inter-municipal cooperation (IMC) in these mechanisms. Based on a dataset of 29,873 French municipalities over the period 2016-2018, we make use of stochastic frontier analysis to estimate a measure of municipal spending efficiency and investigate how it is affected by borrowing size/functions. Our findings show that smaller municipalities benefit from the perks of agglomeration of their neighbors regardless of the IMC, as expected. However, bigger municipalities within an IMC group are those that benefit the most from borrowing functions from their smaller neighbors, casting a shadow over their performance.

title: Smarter M&A for U.S. Competitiveness: Lessons from a U.S. Corporate Development Playbook

detail.title: Smarter M&A for U.S. Competitiveness: Lessons from a U.S. Corporate Development Playbook
detail.abstract: Mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are a cornerstone of U.S. corporate growth, with global deal volume reaching $3.4 trillion in 2024. Yet, a persistent paradox undermines this activity: studies consistently show that 70–75% of mergers fail to achieve their intended synergies, eroding shareholder value and national competitiveness. This paper argues that the adoption of structured, standardized playbooks—codifying financial rigor, strategic benchmarking, and disciplined evaluation—can significantly improve M&A outcomes. Drawing from direct experience within a U.S.-based corporate development team, this analysis presents two applied cases: 1) the due diligence for a European luxury technology acquisition, featuring multi-million-dollar synergy modeling and sensitivity analysis, and 2) a strategic review of the $30 billion global automotive audio sector, benchmarking U.S. firms against global competitors and disruptive entrants. These cases demonstrate that embedding disciplined frameworks into the M&A process is not merely a corporate best practice but a strategic imperative for safeguarding U.S. innovation and economic leadership.

title: Forecasting the U.S. Employment Report and Trading SPY Options: A Data-Driven Strategy with Risk-Controlled Hedging
affiliations: and Independent author

detail.title: Forecasting the U.S. Employment Report and Trading SPY Options: A Data-Driven Strategy with Risk-Controlled Hedging
detail.abstract: The U.S. Employment Situation (Nonfarm Payrolls, NFP¹) is a high-impact release that consistently drives short-term volatility in equity markets. Investors often anticipate this event through elevated implied volatility² in index options, creating an opportunity to trade around the announcement. This paper develops a practical, two-step framework: first, a structured forecasting approach³ using timely labor-market indicators (ADP, jobless claims, ISM employment, Challenger job-cuts, and survey data) to form expectations for the monthly payroll release; second, a focused options strategy on SPY weekly contracts that monetizes the typical IV crush⁴ following the report. Our analysis favors a short straddle⁵ as the baseline strategy, given that implied volatility often overstates realized market moves on NFP days. However, recognizing the inherent tail risk of selling naked volatility, we integrate a hedging plan⁶: adding protective wings (iron condor/butterfly), using delta hedging⁷ with SPY futures, or overlaying correlated exposures (e.g., QQQ) to mitigate directional risk. Using September 2025 as a case study, we demonstrate how this combined approach offers a replicable playbook: forecast the labor data, gauge expected move versus implied move, execute the volatility trade, and contain risk through structured hedging.

title: My Research on the Siemens Case Study: Core Problems and Strategic Solutions Identified Through Academic Inquiry

detail.abstract: This research presents a strategic analysis of Siemens AG, identifying key operational challenges in supply chain management, project delivery, operational technology cybersecurity, and sustainability. Using frameworks such as Kingman's Law, the Bullwhip Effect, Earned Value Management, and IEC 62443, the study proposes digital and data-driven interventions—Integrated S&OP, Digital Twins, Centralized PMO, and Zero-Trust Architecture—to enhance operational performance and sustainability outcomes. The paper provides a phased roadmap and quantitative performance impact expectations to support Siemens’ transformation toward operational excellence.

title: A Structural Decomposition and Path Analysis of Embodied Carbon in ASEAN High-Value Exports: A Comparative Assessment of MRIO Database Methodologies
affiliations: ClimateActionX and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Structural Decomposition and Path Analysis of Embodied Carbon in ASEAN High-Value Exports: A Comparative Assessment of MRIO Database Methodologies
detail.abstract: This study investigates the embodied carbon emissions in high-value exports from key ASEAN economies through a comparative analysis of Multi-Regional Input-Output (MRIO) database methodologies. Using both EXIOBASE and Eora databases, we conduct structural decomposition analysis (SDA) and structural path analysis (SPA) to examine the carbon footprint of electronics and textile sectors from Vietnam, Thailand, and Malaysia during 2015-2020. Our findings reveal significant methodological disparities between MRIO databases, with EXIOBASE consistently reporting 23-35% higher embodied carbon estimates compared to Eora for the same trade flows. The electronics sector demonstrates the highest carbon intensity per unit of export value, with Vietnam's electronics exports embodying 2.8 kg CO₂ per USD of export value (EXIOBASE) versus 2.1 kg CO₂ per USD (Eora). Structural decomposition analysis identifies production technology differences and supply chain complexity as primary drivers of database variations. The textile sector shows more consistent results across databases, with emissions ranging from 1.4-1.8 kg CO₂ per USD of export value. These methodological differences have profound implications for international climate policy, carbon border adjustments, and corporate scope 3 emissions accounting. The study contributes to the growing literature on consumption-based carbon accounting while highlighting the urgent need for harmonized MRIO methodologies in global carbon footprint assessments.

title: Market Power, Expectations, and Asset Prices
affiliations: Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management and Northwestern University - Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences

detail.title: Market Power, Expectations, and Asset Prices
detail.abstract: Recent asset pricing research highlights subjective expectations of long-run profit growth as a key driver of return variation. We show that these expectations—and their deviations from full-information rational expectations—systematically depend on firms' market power. Using U.S. Census LBD data and analyst forecasts, we find that product market power amplifies and prolongs overreaction, while labor market power dampens it. We also document that firm-level overreactions are an order of magnitude larger than aggregate overreactions. Embedding these heterogeneities in a macro-finance model reproduces core asset pricing moments—high excess returns, volatility, and predictable reversals—and shows that distorted expectations, interacting with heterogeneous market power, generate procyclical misallocation and amplify macro-financial fluctuations.

title: Towards Robust Financial Integration: A Tale of Australia and Korea

detail.title: Towards Robust Financial Integration: A Tale of Australia and Korea

keywords: financial integration JEL Classification Numbers: F31

contentType.other: Human-Centered Constitution and Economy Initiative Working Paper No. 2025–01 First circulated: August 2015 Reissued: October 2025

detail.abstract: Robust financial integration presupposes the existence of well-functioning markets for hedging currency exposures. For example, large domestic banks engage in global banking, especially swap-covered FX borrowing, as in Australia. There, they not only provide firms with long-term local currency credits in excess of domestic deposits, but also create inside money denominated in foreign currency through increasing turnovers of FX swaps. In contrast, in the absence of such markets as in Korea, which has maintained a policy of currency non-internalization, cross-currency and FX swap markets can hardly develop vis-à-vis capital markets. Local firms remain exposed to foreign currency risks, and the central bank is pressured to accumulate reserves to prepare for sudden reversals of capital in lieu of private banks. The precautionary accumulation under a floating exchange rate regime, however, ends up facilitating procyclical capital flows.

title: The Tale of Two Climate Risks in Latin America: The Perspective of the NGFS Climate Scenarios
affiliations: I am currently a Visiting Senior Fellow at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE). and WU Vienna University of Economics and Business

detail.title: The Tale of Two Climate Risks in Latin America: The Perspective of the NGFS Climate Scenarios
detail.abstract: This article investigates physical and transition risks for Latin America using as benchmarks the 2023 models and results from the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS). We show that the NGFS has room for improvement when it comes to the usability of its models, especially in the context of Latin America. First, the need to reduce the existence of extremely large and potentially uninformative uncertainty ranges across models (e.g. for the estimate of the carbon price). Second, the need to account for the fact that the future will not look like the past in model calibrations. Third, in the context of physical risks only, the improvement of the hazard suite (to include, e.g. sea-level rise and wildfires) and the consideration of tail risks. Considering these limitations, meeting the 2050 Net Zero emissions objective in Latin America is going to be challenging. It will depend crucially on energy demand and consumption, as well as the use of land in terms of forestry and agriculture. GDP impacts from the transition will likely be negative and worsened by high physical risks, making Latin America worse off than the USA and the EU in the Net Zero 2050 scenario. Our article aims to help the NGFS in the quest to improve its models, and policymakers, especially in Latin America, in better understanding climate risks and finding adequate policy tools to tackle them.

detail.abstract: Agriculture remains one of the major enterprises of Alabama's economy. Alabama is historically known for its cotton production. title: Street Markets, Beauty Salons and Lunchboxes: The Real Entrepreneurship of Brazilian Urban Peripheries
affiliations: Independent Researcher and

detail.title: Street Markets, Beauty Salons and Lunchboxes: The Real Entrepreneurship of Brazilian Urban Peripheries
detail.abstract:
The popular economy in Brazilian urban peripheries constitutes one of the most dynamic yet most invisible phenomena of the national reality. This article analyzes how informal workers — street vendors, open market sellers, beauty salons, home-cooked lunchboxes, artisanal confectionery, app drivers and delivery workers, moto-taxi operators, and digital micro-entrepreneurs — sustain a significant share of the economy despite structural precariousness. The central objective is to highlight the role of these micro-entrepreneurs while problematizing the structural factors driving the growth of informality, such as limited access to education, wage stagnation, rising cost of living, inflation of essential goods, and restricted access to affordable credit.
The research adopts a qualitative and exploratory approach, combined with statistical data from official sources (IBGE, SEBRAE, IPEA, DIEESE) and direct empirical observation in peripheral communities. The dialogue with authors such as Jessé Souza, Ricardo Antunes, Milton Santos, Hernando de Soto, and Amartya Sen provides a theoretical framework articulating social invisibility, labor precarization, peripheral creativity, and the absence of real freedoms.
The findings indicate that the popular economy:
1. Moves billions of reais annually, though under-registered in fiscal and statistical systems;
2. Functions as a survival network for unemployed individuals, retirees, and formal workers seeking complementary income;
3. Intersects with illicit economies, as in the case of moto-taxis in territories under criminal control;
4. Relies heavily on digital tools (WhatsApp, Instagram, Shopee, iFood) as contemporary “public squares” for commerce.
The article concludes that the popular economy is simultaneously an expression of resilience and a critique of the structural failures of the Brazilian state and economic model. Recognizing its centrality is essential for inclusive public policies that expand access to education, credit, and social protection, transforming survival strategies into sustainable development pathways.

title: Learning to Unlearn: Education as a Remedy for Misspecified Beliefs
affiliations: , National Research University Higher School of Economics (Moscow) - International College of Economics and Finance and CREST Ecole Polytechnique

detail.title: Learning to Unlearn: Education as a Remedy for Misspecified Beliefs
detail.abstract: We study education as a remedy for misspecified beliefs in a canonical sequential sociallearning model. Uneducated agents misinterpret action histories-treating actions as if they were independent signals and, potentially, overstating signal precision-while educated agents use the correct likelihoods (and may also enjoy higher private precision). We define a misspecified-belief PBE and show existence with a simple structure: education is a cutoff in the realized cost and actions are threshold rules in a single log-likelihood index. A closed-form value-of-education statistic compares the accuracy of the educated versus uneducated decision at any history; this yields transparent conditions for self-education. When a misspecified process sustains an incorrect cascade, uniformly positive private value and a positive flip probability imply that education breaks the cascade almost surely in finite time, with an explicit bound on expected break time. We quantify welfare gains from making education available and show how small per-education subsidies sharply raise de-cascading probabilities and improve discounted welfare. Extensions cover imperfect observability of education choices and a planner who deploys history-dependent subsidies.

title: Pakistan's Fiscal Trap: Can we End the Cycle of Endless Consolidation?
affiliations: The Planning Commission of Pakistan

detail.title: Pakistan's Fiscal Trap: Can we End the Cycle of Endless Consolidation?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no personal or financial relationship linked with this research paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: There are no ethics issues associated with this research paper.
declarations.funderStatement: I have no funder(s) associated with this research paper.

detail.abstract: This Policy Brief critically examines Pakistan's FY26 federal budget and its macroeconomic implications within the medium-term IMF-supported framework. It argues that the current fiscal strategy-described as 'fiscal consolidation'-in practice functions as prolonged fiscal repression, prioritizing debt servicing over economic recovery, investments and social protection. Using IMF baseline projections for FY26-FY30, the Brief demonstrates that structural constraints, including the 7th NFC Award and the National Fiscal Pact (NFP), have effectively trapped the federal budget in a cycle of borrowing and regressive taxation. Counterfactual simulations show that without radical institutional and debt restructuring, the federal government's fiscal policy will remain encumbered by 'forever' consolidation with no credible terminal point. The Brief outlines an alternative roadmap to recalibrate the fiscal framework: revising the NFC Award, institutionalizing debt servicing as a first charge, restructuring domestic debt, rationalizing the tax burden, legislating borrowing constraints, and strengthening budgetary governance. These measures aim to liberate fiscal policy from structural entrapment, synchronize it with independent monetary policy, and restore its countercyclical role to enable sustainable, inclusive growth.

title: Coordination in Time
affiliations: Chapman University - The George L. Argyros College of Business and Economics, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Economic History and

detail.title: Coordination in Time
detail.abstract: We study how well people are able to solve pure coordination problems in continuous time. Subjects decide whether and when to pay a cost to go to market with their goods and earn money only if another person shows up at the same time. We show that coordination failure is common in a baseline, and we introduce treatments that feature public coordination devices (meant to mimic clocks) and assess the extent to which coordination improves when such devices are provided via different institutions. A publicly provided device outperforms a variety of privately provided alternatives. Our evidence suggests this is because reliable public provision eliminates uncertainty about whether (and how many) other people expect to observe the coordinating signal.

title: Community Surveillance and Property Insurance Risk: Assessing Loss Mitigation Effects of Ring Neighbors
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences, Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences, University of North Dakota - College of Business & Public Administration - Department of Economics and University of North Dakota

detail.title: Community Surveillance and Property Insurance Risk: Assessing Loss Mitigation Effects of Ring Neighbors
detail.abstract: Crimes relevant to home insurers, such as burglary, vandalism, theft, and arson represent a significant driver of homeowners' insurance claims and loss ratios. This study evaluates whether law enforcement adoption of Ring's Neighbors verified accounts, a digital platform that facilitates community reporting and video sharing, reduces the frequency of these crimes. Using a generalized differencein-differences framework across U.S. law enforcement agencies, statistically significant reductions in crimes relevant to home insurers were found following verified account activation. The estimated effects translate into meaningful reductions in expected claims costs and potential improvements in underwriting performance. Beyond the immediate loss frequency reductions, the findings suggest broader implications for insurers: enhanced predictive accuracy in pricing models, reduced volatility in loss experience, and opportunities for product innovation. These results provide early evidence that digital public safety interventions may serve as scalable, low-cost complements to traditional insurance risk mitigation strategies.

title: Digital Payments and Households' Consumption: A Mental Accounting Interpretation
affiliations: Xiamen University - School of Economics,  and Sichuan University - Business School

detail.title: Digital Payments and Households' Consumption: A Mental Accounting Interpretation

keywords: liquidity constraint Subject classification codes: D1

detail.abstract: We explain the stimulating effect of digital payments on households' consumption using mental accounting theory. With the China Household Finance Survey (CHFS) data in 2017, we empirically identify that households who use digital payments spend 20.63% more than those with alternative payment methods. From the mental accounting perspective, we argue that using digital payments increase consumers' transaction utility, facilitate intentional adjustment of mental accounts, and result in more unplanned consumption. The stimulating effect is more substantial on long-term consumption and among households with low self-control abilities. Moreover, the integrated financial services provide access to liquidity and help smooth consumption.

title: Foreign Aid Shapes Local Urban Development
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Foreign Aid Shapes Local Urban Development
detail.abstract: We examine how foreign aid shapes urban development in Sub-Saharan Africa at the very local level. Using data on 1,643 georeferenced Chinese aid projects, we analyze the effect of aid on the evolution of built surface and volume on 100-meter grids within a 2-kilometer radius microregion. Our staggered difference-in-differences approach reveals that foreign aid projects significantly increase local urbanization, with the effects decreasing with distance from the projects. Treatment effects are mostly driven by residential development, particularly in previously underdeveloped areas. Our findings contribute to the understanding of the consequences of foreign aid on urban transformations in the developing world.

title: Slave Trade and the Spread of Islam in Africa: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: The University of Melbourne, Deakin University, University of Adelaide and Deakin University

detail.title: Slave Trade and the Spread of Islam in Africa: Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract: We investigate an overlooked legacy of the Atlantic slave trade: its indirect role in the spread of Islam in West Africa. We develop a theoretical model to study the dynamics of religious conversion in the face of a changing payoff structure, induced by the introduction of the slave trade. Islamic rulers protected Muslims against enslavement, creating an incentive for conversion among non-Muslims. Coupled with non-linear private returns in the share of co-religionists and intergenerational transfer of religion, our model delivers the existence of multiple, stable steady-states for the share of Muslims in a community, theoretically rationalizing the contemporary religious landscape in West Africa. We assemble newly sourced historical data as well as contemporary survey-based measures on the regional presence of Islam to provide empirical support for our model of religious conversion. This analysis reveals that communities under Islamic rule during 1500-1800 and exposed to Atlantic slavery exhibited differentially higher Muslim presence both after the end of slavery and today.

title: Platform Pricing in Peer-to-Peer Rental Markets with Consumer Role Choice
affiliations: Kyoto Sangyo University and Otemon Gakuin University

detail.title: Platform Pricing in Peer-to-Peer Rental Markets with Consumer Role Choice
detail.abstract:
We develop a micro-founded model of P2P rental markets with endogenous consumer roles, rental transactions, and platform pricing under monopoly and duopoly. Consumers flexibly choose their roles among lending, renting, and self-use, which constrains platform fees and deters standard "divide-and-conquer" pricing. This constraint weakens when product prices are higher or usage intensity is lower, enabling platforms to raise fees.
Platform competition can further erode this flexibility, allowing them to set even higher fees. As a result, consumer surplus and social welfare can be lower under duopoly than under monopoly.

title: Equity Valuation Without DCF
affiliations: Korea University Business School, London School of Economics and London School of Economics

detail.title: Equity Valuation Without DCF
detail.abstract: We introduce discounted alpha---a novel framework for equity valuation. By correcting market prices rather than discounting long-duration cash flows, our approach avoids the discount-rate sensitivity that undermines DCF and uncovers fundamental variation missed by leading methods. Applying our estimates, we find that private equity funds appear to capture substantial CAPM misvaluation, both initially at buyout and subsequently at exit, and that fundamental buy-and-hold funds tilt toward characteristics that predict underpricing but not short-term alphas. Furthermore, biased beliefs embedded in analyst estimates appear to be an important driver of model-implied price distortions. However, despite these pockets of misvaluation, firm equity values are "almost efficient" by Black's (1986) definition.

title: Beyond Competition: Toward Interoperable Monetary Layers in the Age of Tokenization
affiliations: Cracow University of Economics, Anambra State Polytechnic, Mgbakwu and Anambra State Polytechnic, Mgbakwu

detail.title: Beyond Competition: Toward Interoperable Monetary Layers in the Age of Tokenization
detail.abstract: Two parallel but potentially opposing forces in the financial landscape: the worldwide development of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) and rapid development of privately offered tokenized assets and decentralized finance (DeFi). Though with more than 130 countries now looking into CBDCs and the tokenized asset market forecast at $16 trillion by 2030, the dynamic between public and private digital monies is shaping up to be the lifeblood of the future direction of payments, lending and monetary policy. This document examines whether or not these systems can work together, or whether their structural differences will create fragmentation, regulatory friction, and systemic risk. Employing a mixed-methods design that ranges from onchain data analysis, comparative case studies related to major CBDC initiatives (for example, digital euro, digital yuan, Project mBridge, Project Aurum), to interviews with professionalscentral bankers, DeFi developers and regulators-we address three crucial questions: (1) Under what circumstances can CBDCs be used as settlement infrastructure for tokenized assets without compromising monetary policy autonomy? (2) What are the implications of design decisions for CBDCs, in particular, programmability, privacy and access, for alignment with DeFi ecosystems? (3) Which governance mechanisms might align both public and private digital money to support inclusive, efficient and resilient financial markets? Our results favour a "layered monetary architecture," with CBDCs to serve as reliable, low-risk, secure settlement anchors and private tokenized finance to facilitate innovation, access and user-friendly services and innovative user experiences. In this paper, we present the Monetary Layer Compatibility Framework which, as we have mentioned, is a diagnostic instrument for tracking the alignment on five aspects of these criteria: settlement finality, programmability scope, privacy guarantees, access permissions, and regulatory hooks. Based on both empirical evidence and policy analysis, we suggest a "public anchor, private innovation" model that maintains monetary sovereignty and benefits from the productivity gain from tokenization. The paper ends with practical policy recommendations to central banks and international institutions to promote interoperability, reduce disintermediation vulnerabilities and halt financial balkanization.

title: A Blueprint for an Emissions Trading System in Bangladesh: Lessons from Global Precedents

detail.title: A Blueprint for an Emissions Trading System in Bangladesh: Lessons from Global Precedents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a comparative policy analysis based on publicly available data and existing literature. It did not involve human or animal subjects, therefore neither ethics approval nor written consent was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a potential design and implementation of an Emissions Trading System (ETS) for Bangladesh. The purpose of the study is to answer two questions. First, it investigates how prominent global ETS models differ from each other in terms of energy efficiency, economic impact, and emission reduction. Second, it examines how the lessons from these systems can be applied to design a viable ETS for Bangladesh. This research employs a comparative policy analysis framework, examining case studies of EU ETS, the US EPA Sulfur Dioxide Program, China Regional Pilot ETS, Mexico ETS Pilot, Korea ETS and California Cap-and-Trade System. The systemic relationships of factors such as Cap Setting and Allocation, Trading Competitiveness and Measures, Sectoral Coverage, Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) are evaluated for each ETS, and the learnings are aggregated to inform a comprehensive system for Bangladesh. The study proposes that a phased implementation for select high-emission industries with competitive trading and reserve mechanisms would be an ideal pilot for Bangladesh. The proposed framework aims to balance Bangladesh's urgent need for emission reduction with its imperative for economic development. The study concludes by outlining a specific set of mechanisms for a possible ETS in Bangladesh and suggests future research directions involving mathematical modeling and synthetic data to predict the pilot's environmental and economic impacts.

title: Application of Deep Reinforcement Learning to At-the-Money S&P 500 Options Hedging
affiliations: University of Warsaw, University of Warsaw - Faculty of Economic Sciences and TripleSun

detail.title: Application of Deep Reinforcement Learning to At-the-Money S&P 500 Options Hedging
detail.abstract: This paper explores the application of deep Q-learning to hedging at-the-money options on the S&P 500 index. We develop an agent based on the Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) algorithm, trained to simulate hedging decisions without making explicit model assumptions on price dynamics. The agent was trained on historical intraday prices of S&P 500 call options across years 2004 to 2024, using a single time series of six predictor variables: option price, underlying asset price, moneyness, time to maturity, realized volatility, and current hedge position. A walk-forward procedure was applied for training, which lead to nearly 17 years of out-of-sample evaluation. The performance of the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent is benchmarked against the Black-Scholes delta hedging strategy over the same time period. We assess both approaches using metrics such as annualized return, volatility, information ratio, and Sharpe ratio. To test models' adaptability, we performed simulations across varying market conditions and added constraints such as transaction costs and risk-awareness penalties. Our results show that the DRL agent can outperform traditional hedging methods, particularly in volatile or high-cost environments, highlighting its robustness and flexibility in practical trading contexts. While the agent consistently outperforms delta hedging, its performance deteriorates when the risk-awareness parameter is higher. We also observed that the longer the time interval used for volatility estimation, the more stable the results.

title: International Law as Extended Phenotype: Globalist and Sovereigntist Memeplexes Competing Through Legal Artifacts (2000-2025)

detail.title: International Law as Extended Phenotype: Globalist and Sovereigntist Memeplexes Competing Through Legal Artifacts (2000-2025)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author was Corporate and Legal Affairs Manager at Alto Paraná S.A. (Argentina's largest forestry company, now named Arauco Argentina S.A.) and Vice President of the Argentine Forestry Association (AFOA) during the Botnia conflict period (2005-2010). Alto Paraná operated pulp mill technology identical to the disputed Botnia facility and publicly supported the project. This insider perspective informed the ethnographic analysis of the Botnia case (Section 3) but did not influence case selection, data verification, or outcome coding for the broader 60-case dataset. The author held no diplomatic role and received no compensation from Uruguay, Finland, Botnia/UPM, or any party to the ICJ proceedings. Current research (2025) is conducted as independent legal scholar with no institutional affiliations or financial interests in forestry, pulp industry, or international tribunals.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzes publicly available legal documents, tribunal rulings, treaties, and news reports. No human subjects participated in this research. No ethics approval was required under standard social science research protocols, as all data sources are public record (ICJ judgments, EU Commission reports, IACHR decisions, academic publications, verified news archives). The dataset contains no personal data, confidential information, or materials requiring informed consent.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All data collection, verification, and analysis were conducted independently by the author without financial support from universities, foundations, governments, or private entities.

keywords: institutional competition JEL Codes: K33 (International Law)

detail.abstract:
This paper applies Dawkins's extended phenotype framework to international law, arguing that legal institutions—treaties, tribunals, judicial decisions—are not mere "representations" of political ideas but material artifacts (treaties as physical documents, tribunals as institutional infrastructures) constructed by competing memeplexes. 

Using a verified dataset of 60 transnational conflicts (2000-2025), with the Argentina-Uruguay Botnia pulp mill case (2006-2010) as paradigmatic I examine how globalist and sovereigntist memeplexes produce distinct phenotypic legal artifacts through institutional competition. 

The International Court of Justice's Botnia ruling (2010), EU Article 7 procedures against Poland/Hungary, and Latin American environmental tribunals are analyzed as extended phenotypes—physical constructs that extend the replicative capacity of their underlying memeplexes, analogous to beaver dams or spider webs in biological systems. This framework reveals international law not as neutral norm-setting but as an evolutionary battlefield where memetic fitness determines which legal artifacts persist, replicate, and shape future conflicts. 

The dataset includes 22 European sovereignty crises (migration, rule of law, austerity) and 8 Latin American extractive conflicts involving international tribunals, demonstrating systematic patterns in phenotypic expression across legal families and geographies.

reference: Ian Allen, The War on Trade: Applying the WTO Security Exceptions to Economic Security Measures, 45 NW. J. INT'L L. & BUS. 157 (2025).
title: The War on Trade: Applying the WTO Security Exceptions to Economic Security Measures Economic Security Measures
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The War on Trade: Applying the WTO Security Exceptions to Economic Security Measures Economic Security Measures

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ian Allen, The War on Trade: Applying the WTO Security Exceptions to Economic Security Measures, 45 NW. J. INT'L L. & BUS. 157 (2025).

detail.abstract:
This article examines the efficacy of the WTO treaties' security exception provisions in curbing abusive appeals to national security to justify otherwise impermissible trade measures. It specifically explores whether GATT Article XXI and its sister provisions establish objectively discernible prerequisite conditions for their invocation, how far Member discretion extends in defining "essential security interests," and whether the WTO dispute system offers sufficiently objective legal standards to prevent abuse of the security exceptions.

Building on existing scholarship, this article employs a comprehensive interpretive analysis of all available means under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT) and integrates not just the landmark Russia – Traffic in Transit report, but also the recent United States – Steel and Aluminum and United States – Origin Marking cases of December 2022. This interpretive exercise identifies a uniform analytical framework running through each WTO Panel report reviewing invocations of the security exceptions and applies that framework to critique the U.S. position on the issue. Under this interpretive framework, this article ultimately determines whether and to what extent the WTO security exceptions including GATT Article XXI(b)(iii) justify discriminatory and anti-competitive trade measures purportedly imposed in the name of “economic security.”

title: Bank Internal Credit Ratings Bias and Borrower Financial Reporting Quality
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and University of New Mexico - Robert O. Anderson Schools of Management

detail.title: Bank Internal Credit Ratings Bias and Borrower Financial Reporting Quality
