Central banks specify which assets banks can pledge as collateral to obtain short-term central bank funding. This is referred to as central bank collateral policy and involves a trade-off between supplying sufficient liquidity to banks and exposing itself to losses from accepting risky assets as collateral. Emission taxes affect this trade-off by reducing productivity in the non-financial sector, such that the corporate default rate increases and the quality of collateral deteriorates. High emission taxes also reduce investment, debt issuance and, hence, the amount of collateral available to banks. This decline in the quantity of collateral is more pronounced if emission tax shocks are very persistent or permanent. It is therefore optimal to relax collateral policy in the longer run, where the collateral quantity channel dominates, and to tighten collateral policy after a transitory emission tax shock, in order to offset the short run reduction in collateral quality.

title: Social Trading, Correlated Retail Investing and Non-Fundamental Speculation
affiliations: Universitaet Regensburg

detail.title: Social Trading, Correlated Retail Investing and Non-Fundamental Speculation
detail.abstract: This paper shows that, in a setup á la Kyle (1985), correlated retail trading opens up new profit opportunities for professional investors at the expense of retail investors. Additionally, it demonstrates that market quality can benefit through higher market liquidity and higher price efficiency. Our results lend support to concerns that social trading via Finfluencers and stock message boards harms rather than benefits retail investors.

title: Culture and Constitutional Compliance
affiliations: University of Hamburg - Institute of Law and Economics, University of Warsaw, University of Warsaw and University of Hamburg - Institute of Law & Economics

detail.title: Culture and Constitutional Compliance
detail.abstract: Constitutions as the formal foundation of a country’s legal and political system have important economic and political effects. Yet, we still know little about why constitutions set effective constraints on politicians in some societies, while being largely disregarded in others. Here, we ask if national culture matters for constitutional compliance. We study a cross-section of 115 countries, making use of novel indicators of constitutional compliance. We find that societies with a more individualistic population exhibit higher levels of compliance. These results are robust and extend to instrumental variable estimations. They imply a novel transmission channel from cultural traits to long-term economic development: individualistic national culture increases the credibility of constitutional self-commitments. Our analysis also supports the more general idea that the effects of formal institutions depend on the informal institutional environment in which they are embedded. Regarding religion, our results are consistent with past research that attributes the lack of development in the modern Muslim world to deficient institutional quality.

title: Regional Loan Market Structure, Bank Lending Rates and Monetary Transmission
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Regional Loan Market Structure, Bank Lending Rates and Monetary Transmission
detail.abstract: The present paper utilizes AnaCredit loan-level data to examine the impact of regional loan market structure on lending rates. The analysis focuses on newly issued loans to small non-financial corporations in the euro area during the monetary policy tightening phase of 2022 and 2023. The findings suggest that banks tend to charge higher lending rates when they possess larger regional market shares. This outcome is driven by differences between banks rather than by individual banks adjusting their lending rates to regional market conditions. Overall, there is no strong evidence that market power conveyed by higher regional market concentration impeded the transmission of the monetary policy tightening to lending rates. If anything, there are indications that this type of market power may hinder the short-term pass-through of the unexpected component of monetary policy.

title: Fiscal Policy and Politicians' Term Length
affiliations: Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan, Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan - Graduate School in Public Economics (DEFAP) and

detail.title: Fiscal Policy and Politicians' Term Length
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the causal effect of the term length of political executives on economic policy outcomes. To establish causality, we exploit the staggered adoption of four-year terms for governors across US states, using data for the period 1937–2008. We find that increasing governors’ tenure in office from two years to four years reduced state expenditures and revenues by approximately 0.3–0.5 percentage points of GDP. The effect on state finances is primarily driven by a reduction of current spending and grants from the federal government, and it is concentrated in states where the incumbent governor expects fierce competition in the next election. Lastly, we discuss the implications of longer terms for macroeconomic stabilization, political budget cycles, and intergovernmental resource allocation.

title: Gratitude in Fundraising: Do ‘Thank You in Advanceʼ and Handwritten Thank-You Notes Impact Fundraising Success?
affiliations: WZB Berlin Social Science Center, Wissenschaftszentrum Berlin für Sozialforschung (WZB) and German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin)

detail.title: Gratitude in Fundraising: Do ‘Thank You in Advanceʼ and Handwritten Thank-You Notes Impact Fundraising Success?
detail.abstract: While almost all charities rely on a set of donor appreciation strategies, their effectiveness for the success of fundraising campaigns is underresearched. Through two preregistered field studies conducted in collaboration with a leading German opera house (N=10,000), we explore the significance of expressing gratitude and examine two different approaches to doing so. Our first study investigates the impact of a "thank you in advance" statement in fundraising letters, a common strategy among fundraisers. In the second study, we explore the effectiveness of handwritten thank-you postcards versus printed postcards, shedding light on the roles of personalization and handwriting in donor appeals. Our findings challenge conventional wisdom, revealing that neither “thank you in advance” nor handwritten thank-you notes significantly affect donor contributions.

title: Unbundling the Effects of College on First-Job Search: Returns to Majors, Minors, and Extracurriculars
affiliations: Yale University, Rome Economics Doctorate, University of Wisconsin - La Crosse and Auburn University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Unbundling the Effects of College on First-Job Search: Returns to Majors, Minors, and Extracurriculars
detail.abstract: We analyze the initial job-market matching of new US college graduates with a largescale audit study conducted during 2016 and 2017, in which 36,880 resumes of college ´ seniors were submitted to online job postings for business-related positions. We simulate the experience of US college students by incorporating variation in curricular and extracurricular activities. Our analysis reveals significant variation in callback rate returns to majors, with Biology and Economics majors receiving the highest rate, particularly in occupations involving high intensity of analytical and interpersonal skills. However, minors in History and Mathematics have precisely estimated zero effects on callback rates. Internship experiences that are social skills-oriented positively influence callbacks, yet this is not the case for analytical internships. Study abroad experiences enhance callback rates, predominantly in high interpersonal skill-intensive occupations. Listing both programming and data analysis skills significantly boosts callback rates. Our study provides a comprehensive characterization of which features of the college experience are more and less valuable during the high-stakes, first-job matching process.

title: The Tragedy of the Common Heating Bill
affiliations: University of Zurich - Department of Economics and University of Mannheim - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Tragedy of the Common Heating Bill
detail.abstract: We leverage quasi-experimental variation to study how group size influences free-riding behavior within a high-expense environment. When buildings lack apartment-specific heat meters, tenants use simple heuristics to split a common bill. We estimate that the staggered rollout of a corrective technology, “submetering,” reduces heating expenses by 17%, on average. Machine learning techniques uncover substantial heterogeneity, consistent with strategic exit of free-riders and coordination failures in large buildings. Tenants in smaller buildings show minimal response and are surprisingly price elastic. Only a minority of households exploits the free-riding incentives. Targeted submetering policies can be much more cost-effective than universal mandates.

title: Transshipment Hubs, Trade, and Supply Chains
affiliations: Michigan State University, Georgetown University, University of Oregon - Department of Economics and Michigan State University

detail.title: Transshipment Hubs, Trade, and Supply Chains
detail.abstract: The majority of global trade moves by sea through hub-and-spoke shipping networks. We investigate the returns to being a hub country by analyzing how transshipment activity shapes trade and supply chains. We show that most US imports—especially from smaller origin countries—are transshipped via key hubs, and transshipment is positively correlated with the hub’s product-level trade. Leveraging the indirect shipping network structure to construct an instrument, we find that transshipment increases hubs’ imports from origins for which they facilitate trade and exports of downstream goods, highlighting their central role in shaping modern global trade and supply chain dynamics.

title: FX-constrained growth: Fundamentalists, chartists and the dynamic trade-multiplier
affiliations: Bucknell University and University of Siena - Department of Economics and Statistics

detail.title: FX-constrained growth: Fundamentalists, chartists and the dynamic trade-multiplier
detail.abstract: Behavioural finance offers a valuable framework for examining foreign exchange (FX) market dynamics, including puzzles such as excess volatility and fat-tailed distributions. Yet, when it comes to their interaction with the `real' side of the economy, existing scholarship has overlooked a critical feature of developing countries. They cannot trade in their national currencies and need US dollars to access modern production techniques as well as maintain consumption patterns similar to those of wealthier societies. To address this gap, we present a novel heterogeneous agents model from the perspective of a developing economy that distinguishes between speculative and non-speculative sectors in the FX market. We demonstrate that as long as non-speculative demand responds to domestic economic activity, a market-clearing output growth rate exists that, in steady-state, is equal to the ratio between FX supply growth and the income elasticity of demand for foreign assets, i.e., a generalised dynamic trade-multiplier. Numerical simulations reproduce key stylised facts of exchange rate dynamics and economic growth, including distributions that deviate from the typical bell-shaped curve. Data from a sample of Latin American countries reveal that FX fluctuations exhibit similar statistical properties. Furthermore, we employ time-varying parameter estimation techniques to show that the dynamic trade-multiplier closely tracks observed growth rates in these economies.

title: Parental Leave and Intimate Partner Violence
affiliations: University of London, Royal Holloway College - Department of Economics, The Rockwool Foundation Research Unit, University of Copenhagen and University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Parental Leave and Intimate Partner Violence
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of a 2002 Danish parental leave reform on intimate partner violence (IPV) using administrative data on assault-related hospital contacts. Using a regression discontinuity design, we show that extending fully paid leave increased mothers’ leave-taking and substantially reduced IPV, with effects concentrated among less-educated women. The reform also lengthened birth spacing, while separations remained unchanged and earnings effects were modest. The timing and heterogeneity of impacts point to fertility adjustments—rather than exit options or financial relief—as the key mechanism. Parental leave policy thus emerges as an underexplored lever for reducing IPV.

title: The systemic impact of edges in financial networks
affiliations: Government of the Federative Republic of Brazil - Central Bank of Brazil, Government of the Federative Republic of Brazil - Central Bank of Brazil and University of São Paulo (USP)

detail.title: The systemic impact of edges in financial networks
detail.abstract: In this paper, we assess how the stability of financial networks is affected by interconnectedness considering its tiniest variation: the edge. We compute the impact of edges as the percentage difference in the systemic risk (SR) of the whole network caused by the inclusion of that edge. We apply this framework to a thorough Brazilian dataset to compute the impact of bank-firm edges. After observing that (i) edges are heterogeneous regarding their impact on the SR, and (ii) the fraction of edges whose impact on the SR is non-positive increases with the level of the initial shock, we use machine learning techniques to try to predict two variables: the criticality of the edges (defining as critical an edge whose impact on SR is significantly greater than that of the others) and the sign of the edge impact. The level of accuracy obtained in these prediction exercises was very high. These results have important implications for the development macroprudential policies aimed at financial stability. Our framework allows to identify, based on features related to the origin and destination nodes of the edge (i.e., the lending bank and the borrowing firm), whether an additional loan will have a significant and positive impact on the SR.

title: Case summary: Distillers Corporation (SA) Ltd v SA Breweries Ltd & Another; Oude Meester Groep Bpk & Another v SA Breweries Ltd 1976 (3) SA 514 (A)
affiliations: Stellenbosch University

detail.title: Case summary: Distillers Corporation (SA) Ltd v SA Breweries Ltd & Another; Oude Meester Groep Bpk & Another v SA Breweries Ltd 1976 (3) SA 514 (A)

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract: The Appellate Division heard concurrent appeals concerning trade mark infringement (Distillers OUDE MEESTER/MEESTER marks v Breweries MASTERBREW beer) and the expungement of marks. Breweries sought expungement of 13 Distillers marks registered for beer based on continuous non-use for the statutory five-year period (Section 36(1)(b)). TROLLIP JA held that the court of first instance erred by giving undue weight to the policy underlying defensive trade marks (Section 53). The general policy requires use or intention to use the mark, and Distillers extensive use for spirits was insufficient to save the beer registrations. The Court granted expungement and upheld the order for a disclaimer regarding the exclusive use of the word MEESTER, finding it to be a non-distinctive, laudatory term equivalent to MASTER.  The appeal against the infringement ruling failed and both appeals were dismissed

title: Instrumental Freedoms and the Toga Cartel in Colombia
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS

detail.title: Instrumental Freedoms and the Toga Cartel in Colombia
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the "Cartel de la Toga" scandal in Colombia from the perspective of Amartya Sen's theoretical postulates on instrumental freedoms and the concepts of agency and choice. It examines how this phenomenon of judicial corruption violated the five essential freedoms-political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, guarantees of transparency, and protective security-that underpin human development and democratic legitimacy. From an interdisciplinary perspective, it links the institutional effects of corruption to the weakening of citizen capacities and public trust in the Colombian constitutional state.

title: Modelling Control of Corruption in Health Spending Efficiency Evaluation at the Country-Level
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Econometrics and Business Statistics, Monash University and Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics

detail.title: Modelling Control of Corruption in Health Spending Efficiency Evaluation at the Country-Level
detail.abstract: The efficiency of health spending in a country is critical for the well-being of its citizens. Previous studies highlight that corruption, which is one of the critical indicators of governance, is not only prevalent in many countries but also a significant contributor to inefficiencies in health spending. Exploiting this finding, this study introduces a new variable returns to scale input-oriented DEA model for evaluating health spending performance across 178 countries. The conventional DEA model includes corruption control as a non-discretionary input, per capita health spending as a discretionary input, and life expectancy at birth as the output. The conventional DEA model is modified to ensure that the corruption control index of a role model country for an inefficient country will not be worse than that of the inefficient country itself. However, in the new DEA model, the efficiency scores may not be obtained with reference to the same frontier and hence are not comparable. Therefore, this paper proposes a new efficiency measure where the efficiency score obtained in the conventional DEA model is adjusted with the efficiency score obtained in the new DEA model. A cross-sectional analysis of 178 countries using 2020 data reveals significant differences in countries' rankings based on the efficiency scores obtained in the conventional DEA model and with the new measure. An important finding of this paper is that the adjusted efficiency scores can be effectively used for benchmarking when the efficiency frontiers vary between decision-making units.

title: Untangling Illiquidity: Optimal Asset Allocation with Private Asset Classes
affiliations: University of Amsterdam

detail.title: Untangling Illiquidity: Optimal Asset Allocation with Private Asset Classes
detail.abstract: Strategic Asset Allocation in practice relies almost exclusively on mean – variance optimizations. This paper develops a dynamic portfolio choice model that embeds stochastic liquidity constraints into the SAA process. I show that ignoring asset illiquidity risk leads to systematic overallocation to private asset classes and exposes investors to severe consumption risk when liquidity shocks occur. Gains from investing in private assets are substantially tempered once illiquidity is accounted for. These results highlight the need to move beyond variance-only risk metrics and incorporate asset liquidity as a first-order consideration in the strategic portfolio design of investors considering private asset classes. In contrast to prior literature, which often adds complexity to the cash-flow modeling of illiquid assets but remains stylized in portfolio composition, I extend the framework to a realistic multi-asset universe and develop a fast numerical algorithm tailored for practical implementation.

title:
Unemployment and the U.S. Economy: Rate, Claims, and Duration in a Changing Policy 
Environment (2024–2025 Forecast)
affiliations: American International University

detail.title:
Unemployment and the U.S. Economy: Rate, Claims, and Duration in a Changing Policy 
Environment (2024–2025 Forecast)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, professional, or financial relationships that could have influenced the conduct, findings, or interpretation of this research. This study was conducted independently for academic purposes as part of an economics coursework requirement. The author has no conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or personal data collection. All information used in this research was derived from secondary data and publicly available economic databases. Therefore, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All materials, data, and resources used in the preparation of this paper were obtained from publicly available sources such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the U.S. Department of Labor, the Federal Reserve, and other open-access databases.

detail.abstract:
Unemployment remains one of the most powerful indicators that shows the real health and direction of an economy. This paper studies the relationship between unemployment and overall economic performance in the United States from January 2024 through August 2025. The research applies a qualitative and quantitative descriptive analysis combined with trend forecasting to understand how the unemployment rate, new jobless claims, and the duration of unemployment reflect the nation’s short-term and long-term stability. Data for this study were collected from official sources including the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the U.S. Department of Labor, the Federal Reserve, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the World Bank.

Findings show that the U.S. labor market in mid-2025 remains stable but cooling, with the national unemployment rate at 4.1 percent, compared to 3.6 percent in 2024. The broader U-6 unemployment measure stands at 7.5 percent, indicating underemployment concerns. Weekly initial claims average around 235,000, which is still below recession levels, while long-term unemployment makes up 25.7 percent of all jobless persons. Wage growth of 3.8 percent and inflation around 2.5 percent suggest that the Federal Reserve’s “soft landing” policy is functioning effectively.

The analysis concludes that although regional variations and long-term joblessness persist, the U.S. economy demonstrates resilience supported by strong consumer spending and gradual policy adjustments. The next 6–12 months are projected to bring mild moderation rather than contraction, with unemployment expected to stabilize near 4.0 percent by mid-2026. Policy implications emphasize workforce retraining, small-business credit support, and digital skill development to ensure inclusive and sustainable employment growth.

title: Mean-Field Price Formation on Trees
affiliations: University of Tokyo - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Mean-Field Price Formation on Trees
detail.abstract: In this work, we combine the mean-field game theory with the classical idea of binomial tree framework, pioneered by Sharpe and Cox, Ross & Rubinstein, to solve the equilibrium price formation problem for the stock. For agents with exponential utilities and recursive utilities of exponential type, we prove the existence of a unique mean-field equilibrium and derive an explicit formula for equilibrium transition probabilities of the stock price by restricting its trajectories onto a binomial tree. The agents are subject to stochastic terminal liabilities and incremental endowments, both of which are dependent on unhedgeable common and idiosyncratic factors, in addition to the stock price path. Finally, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the qualitative effects of these components on the equilibrium price distribution.

title: Sentiment and Environmental Performance
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Utrecht University - School of Economics

detail.title: Sentiment and Environmental Performance
detail.abstract: We identify a novel behavioral driver of environmental performance. An increase in countrylevel consumer sentiment leads to sustained reduction in emission intensity over a multiyear horizon. Since consumer sentiment increases investment, productivity, energy efficiency, and stock market returns, a plausible explanation is that firms can afford to engage in costly reduction of emissions in a buoyant market. The effect tapers off over time and is stronger in countries where sentiment is a more reliable signal for the state of the economy. Our results suggest that policies boosting economic expectations yield substantial environmental benefits.

title: Are export tax rebates patronage for Chinese firms?
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE) and Sichuan University - Business School

detail.title: Are export tax rebates patronage for Chinese firms?
detail.abstract: This paper examines the nexus between export tax rebates and productivity using Chinese firm-level data from 2000 to 2007. The empirical findings indicate that a one percentage point decrease in export tax rebate rates increases the total factor productivity (TFP) of a firm by about 0.1 percentage points. We explore the possible mechanisms that explain this nexus and attribute it to the allocation effect of export tax rebate policy; that is, export tax rebates prevent low-productivity firms from exiting the market and further reallocate resources and economic activities to them. In addition, a decrease in rebate rates significantly encourages the TFP growth of surviving firms and leads to an increase in aggregate TFP. Specifically, throughout 2000-07, the declining rebate rates accounted for 5.23% of the rise in the aggregate TFP, and the between-firm effect was 3.85%, which is much larger than the within effect.

title: Feature Configuration Effects in DRL Portfolio Management: A Risk-Focused Evaluation under Market Stress
affiliations: Zeppelin University

detail.title: Feature Configuration Effects in DRL Portfolio Management: A Risk-Focused Evaluation under Market Stress
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents can effectively use financial feature information for risk-aware portfolio management. We design a controlled experimental framework that compares four feature configurations: BARRA-derived systematic risk information, technical indicators, their combination, and a no-feature baseline. Using the Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) algorithm across 800 independently trained agents on randomly sampled 30-stock S&P 500 portfolios, we evaluate out-of-sample performance during the volatile 2022 market and assess statistical significance via paired permutation tests. The BARRA-derived information provides significant downside protection, improving maximum drawdown by 0.71% (p = 0.02) relative to the baseline, while technical indicators do not offer significant benefit alone or in combination. These results indicate that DRL agents can leverage systematic risk information to manage tail risk, and that targeted feature selection based on financial theory may be more effective than indiscriminate feature augmentation.

title: Importing Pop Idols? Socioeconomic Consequences of K-pop Boom in the US
affiliations: Yonsei University and

detail.title: Importing Pop Idols? Socioeconomic Consequences of K-pop Boom in the US
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the socioeconomic effects of K-pop's rising popularity in the United States during the mid-2010s, when the genre first gained mainstream traction. Our empirical strategy exploits geographic variation in K-pop exposure across U.S. metropolitan areas. To address potential endogeneity, we instrument metropolitanlevel K-pop popularity with pre-existing Asian population shares and the inflow of Asian immigrants. The findings show that areas more exposed to K-pop experienced adverse impacts on the local performing arts industry, consistent with consumer preferences in mass media shifting toward foreign music genres. Beyond cultural substitution, K-pop's influence also extended to broader sociological outcomes, including (i) increased online search activity for K-beauty, (ii) higher imports of cosmetics and CDs from South Korea, and (iii) a rise in Asian intermarriage rates.

title: Principal Competence and Organizational Candor: How Moderate Expertise Breeds Cover-Ups
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: Principal Competence and Organizational Candor: How Moderate Expertise Breeds Cover-Ups
detail.abstract: Across healthcare, aviation, and corporate settings, partial improvements in oversight or leadership often lead to more sophisticated cover-ups rather than more candor. Conventional wisdom suggests that more competent principals improve evaluation and decision-making, yet prior theoretical work also shows that competence can backfire. We study how a principal's competence shapes communication and welfare and establish a non-monotonic impact of competence that reconciles these views. In our model, a principal jointly evaluates project quality and agent competence based on the agent's report. Strategic incentives-in particular, fear of replacement-distort information transmission, and the form of distortion depends on the principal's competence. Moderate competence induces cover-ups (reporting good news when the truth is bad), while high competence induces crying wolf (reporting bad news when the truth is good). As leaders become more competent, agents' incentives to act as yes-men-recommending the status quo rather than replacement-intensify. This dynamic reduces welfare when the principal is moderately competent but increases welfare when the principal is highly competent, yielding a U-shaped relationship between competence and welfare. These findings highlight how partial improvements in competence can worsen outcomes and suggest institutional remedies such as separating evaluation tasks or protecting whistleblowers.

title: Can the World Survive without Internet for One Day?
affiliations: Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School

detail.title: Can the World Survive without Internet for One Day?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE

declarations.funderStatement: NONE

detail.abstract: This paper presents a review of the consequences of a full collapse of the internet access worldwide and its profound effects on both economic structures and social dynamics. The study explores how the global economy increasingly depends on the internet uses as a critical driver of productivity, innovation, and interconnected markets. It emphasizes the high dependency in shaping trade, financial transactions, and business models, while also considering its broader social implications such as communication, education, and cultural exchange. By conducting a focused analysis, this research highlights the opportunities and challenges created by the pervasive integration of the internet into daily life and economic activity. The findings suggest that internet accessibility not only accelerates economic growth and competitiveness but also introduces new vulnerabilities, inequalities, and governance issues. This paper concludes that understanding the dual impact of the internet both as an enabler of global development and as a source of complex socioeconomic challenges is essential for designing sustainable policies in the digital era.

title: Comparative Analysis of Tourist Flow Trends in Northeast India and South Korea: A Study Based on the Pentagonal Review Matrix for Research
affiliations: Assam University - Department of Business Administration, Jawaharlal Nehru University and Manipur International University

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of Tourist Flow Trends in Northeast India and South Korea: A Study Based on the Pentagonal Review Matrix for Research
detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the tourist inflow trends in Northeast India and South Korea by determining the Seasonal Index (SI). Given the growing concerns about resource scarcity and the need for competent policymakers, determining the SI emerges as an efficient approach. It provides a comprehensive overview for stakeholders to plan and devise policies while educating tourists on the optimal seasons for visiting. The study is structured around three key objectives: determining the Seasonal Index (SI), and recommending strategies to enhance the tourist experience in Northeast India and South Korea. To ensure the quality and depth of the findings, a pentagonal review matrix and descriptive methodology were employed, with secondary data from various sources analyzed to derive meaningful insights. The study introduces the SI as an ideal and data-driven approach for policy and strategy formulation, addressing the current gap in tourism data analysis. The research highlights key issues and informs effective planning strategies. A key takeaway from this study is the critical need for competent stakeholders to develop the best strategies and policies that align with the SI, ensuring resource management and enhanced tourist satisfaction.

title: Beyond State vs. Market: Reframing State Capacity via Autonomy, Inclusion, and Mission-Driven Governance
affiliations: Hacettepe University

detail.title: Beyond State vs. Market: Reframing State Capacity via Autonomy, Inclusion, and Mission-Driven Governance
detail.abstract: This review synthesizes three paradigms: developmental state theory, inclusive institutions, and mission-oriented policy into a unified AIM (Autonomy × Inclusivity × Mission) framework of state capacity. The AIM framework is based upon three works, along with supporting papers, symbolizing each dimension: Milor's France-Turkey comparison, Acemoglu & Robinson's institutional framework, and Mazzucato's entrepreneurial state theory as an empirical anchor. It introduces a new configuration model that reveals how autonomy, inclusivity, and missionorientation interact as complementary rather than competing dimensions of state capacity. We demonstrate through comparative case analysis that optimal state capacity requires balanced achievement across all three dimensions, which is not static and variable as evidenced through historical examples.

title: Data Extraction Taxes
affiliations: University of Tennessee, Knoxville - Winston College of Law

detail.title: Data Extraction Taxes
detail.abstract:
This Article provides a practical framework for states to tax data extraction by adapting severance tax principles that have underpinned the taxation of natural resource extraction for decades. 

Established tax regimes may not adequately capture the value businesses derive from extracting and monetizing user data. As data-the "new gold"-becomes central to all facets of the economy and increases dramatically in value, particularly with the emergence of AI, states are desperately seeking ways to more effectively tax data-centric business models. States have attempted to modernize corporate taxation regimes, and states have enacted new digital advertising tax regimes. This Article, however, suggests that if states seek a separate tax regime to capture the value businesses derive from data monetization, a data extraction tax is the preferred option. 

This Article first analyzes the conceptual and practical difficulties of taxing data as an economic resource. This Article then explores established state severance tax models for natural resources such as precious metals, minerals, oil, and gas, identifying key principles and mechanisms that can be adapted to data extraction. 

Building on these severance tax principles, this Article proposes a comprehensive design for a state-level data extraction tax, addressing critical elements including the appropriate tax base, rate structures, sourcing rules, and collection mechanisms. This analysis further examines potential constitutional limitations on state taxation of data and considers potential federal preemption challenges that might constrain state taxing authority in this domain. 

By offering a detailed blueprint for state-level data taxation grounded in established legal principles, this Article provides policymakers with a practical framework to address business models based on extracting and monetizing user data.

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence and Big Data for Competitive Advantage in Agribusiness Operations
affiliations: Oxford Academy and George Mason University

detail.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence and Big Data for Competitive Advantage in Agribusiness Operations
detail.abstract: Agribusiness today stands at the intersection of digital innovation and sustainable development. Faced with challenges such as climate change, resource depletion, and volatile global markets, the sector must undergo profound transformation. This thesis explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Big Data analytics can be strategically leveraged to create and sustain competitive advantage in agribusiness operations. Adopting a qualitative exploratory design, the research integrates a systematic literature review of 118 peer-reviewed sources with cross-case analysis of digitalagriculture initiatives across both developed and emerging economies. The theoretical framework combines the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Dynamic Capabilities (DC) theories to explain how data-driven capabilities-supported by strong governance, skilled human capital, and adaptive leadership-function as strategic resources. Findings reveal that AI and Big Data deliver competitive advantage through four primary mechanisms: operational efficiency, product differentiation, market responsiveness, and sustainability innovation. However, adoption remains uneven, constrained by high costs, limited infrastructure, and data-governance gaps. The research identifies that enduring advantage emerges not from technology alone, but from a firm's ability to sense opportunities, seize them through innovation, and reconfigure resources continuously. The study contributes theoretically by extending RBV to digital agribusiness contexts and empirically by proposing a conceptual model linking data resources, analytical capabilities, and competitive outcomes. Practically, it provides actionable strategies for managers and policymakers to foster inclusive, ethical, and sustainable digital transformation. The conclusions support the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production).

title: Sustainable Development and the Digital Economy Human-centricity, Sustainability and Resilience in Asia
affiliations: Hasanuddin University, Hasanuddin University and Hasanuddin University

detail.title: Sustainable Development and the Digital Economy Human-centricity, Sustainability and Resilience in Asia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors have no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or animal subjects. All data utilized in the analysis were obtained from publicly available secondary sources, including financial reports, stock exchange data, and patent databases. Therefore, formal ethical approval was not required. The research was conducted in accordance with academic integrity standards, ensuring confidentiality, transparency, and responsible use of data

detail.abstract: This research investigates integrating the digital economy with sustainable business practices in China, focusing on the dynamic nature of digital technology adoption and environmental sustainability within Chinese enterprises. The study aims to recommend effective strategies for enhancing sustainable innovation through digitalization, providing guidance for policymakers, corporate leaders, and managers. By selecting a sample of firms from 2008 to 2022, including data from companies listed on the stock exchange and detailed patent information, the study employs zero-inflated negative binomial regression to address the peculiarities of patent counts accurately. This method avoids the assumptions of linearity of dependent variables and normality of residuals common in many empirical innovation studies. The research confirms a positive relationship between digital adoption and green patents. Notably, there is a significant reduction in environmental outputs from firms operating in China's 'Big Data Comprehensive Pilot Zone,' supporting the argument that policies promoting green innovation are effective. Additionally, the study identifies several key factors influencing the successful implementation of digital technologies and sustainability, including firm size, industry nature, and regional economic characteristics. These findings are crucial for policymakers and managers, emphasizing the importance of digitalization in achieving sustainability goals.

title: Debt Release Strategy for Sustainable Human Development
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics, University of Tuscia and Athens University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Debt Release Strategy for Sustainable Human Development

declarations.ethicsApproval: The research has no empirical section

detail.abstract: We explore the intersection of foreign debt in poor and emerging countries and global climate challenges, proposing a comprehensive strategy to promote both financial and ecological debt sustainability. We sketch the main characteristics of a debt for sustainable development conversion scheme involving multiple stakeholders, including international development banks, private sector actors pursuing net-zero targets, and local communities. Under this scheme, debt relief would be conditional upon investments in renewable energy projects and sustainability initiatives in debtor countries. A main advantage of this scheme over the alternative of unconditional debt relief accompanied by lender subsidized green finance is that the former has features that are mutually beneficial for the counterparts easing the participation constraint of the lender, preventing green moral hazard of the borrower and increasing efficiency in emission reduction. We as well show that related climate investments could reduce global carbon emissions, promote local economic resilience, and address energy poverty.

title: Complexity Theory and Economic Inequality
affiliations: University of Chicago - Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility, Emory University - Department of Economics and University of Michigan - Center for the Study of Complex Systems

detail.title: Complexity Theory and Economic Inequality

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 25-20
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We analyze the potential for complexity theory to produce insights that elucidate the evolution of socioeconomic inequality and point toward effective policies. We position complexity theory as a complement to more traditional economic approaches. Economic models of inequality can fall into four broad categories: models based on individual attributes and technologies, social interaction models, intergenerational models of transfer, and models of institutional and social structure. Within each of these categories, complexity theory can enhance traditional theory. It is of particular value in helping to distinguish between bottom-up systemic and top-down structural causes of inequality. Complexity theory can further enrich our understanding of economic inequality by adopting a complex adaptive system of systems approach in which economic, social, political, and psychosocial systems interact with one another and with institutional and social structures to produce robust inequality, particularly on racial lines.

title: PERCEPTION OF CHALLENGES AND NEEDS REGARDING ANIMAL WELFARE IN LATIN AMERICAN AQUACULTURE
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidad Científica del Sur, IRTA, Autonomous University of Barcelona, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Institute of Marine Sciences, Universidad de Guanajuato, Universidad Técnica Estatal de Quevedo, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Instituto de Ciencias del Mar, Universidad Católica de Temuco, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Institute of Marine Sciences

detail.title: PERCEPTION OF CHALLENGES AND NEEDS REGARDING ANIMAL WELFARE IN LATIN AMERICAN AQUACULTURE
detail.abstract: Aquatic animal welfare (AAW) is increasingly recognized as a critical component of sustainable aquaculture in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). This study aimed to identify the main welfare challenges perceived by LAC stakeholders, including scientists, staff of the Competent National Authorities (CNA) and industry professionals, through a three-day online workshop involving 150 participants and 21 countries. Using topic modelling to analyse responses across four welfare domains (nutrition, environment, health and behaviour), the study revealed that the stakeholders’ most frequently cited concerns related to animal-based welfare indicators, feeding strategies, and sanitary conditions, particularly during early life stages. Key issues included feed quality, stress, mortality, and cannibalism, while reproductive and grow-out stages emphasized spawning, feeding and sanitation. Environmental challenges, such as water quality, stocking density and exposure to predators were highlighted, along with the need for improved veterinary care, disease control and accurate diagnosis. Behavioural welfare responses indicated limited knowledge, the need for better assessment tools and facilities that promote natural behaviours. Slaughter methods emerged as a significant area of concern, with stakeholders emphasizing the importance of capacity building, minimizing stress and suffering, and standardized protocols. Species-specific knowledge was also identified, particularly in nutrition, behaviour, and disease diagnosis. Research priorities included nutrition, stress, water management and environmental impact, while operational improvements focused on standardized management, personnel training, and comprehensive guidance documents. Overall, LAC stakeholders demonstrated a growing awareness of AAW issues and a had strong demand for both theoretical and practical solutions to improve welfare standards in LAC aquaculture.

title: The Moderating Effect of the Sovereign Credit Rating between GDP and Sovereign Debt
affiliations: Sistema Nacional de Investigación, SENACYT, Panamá/Universidad UMECIT Panama

detail.title: The Moderating Effect of the Sovereign Credit Rating between GDP and Sovereign Debt
detail.abstract: Sovereign credit ratings are very important for any national and international economy. While a sovereign credit rating upgrade can encourage international investors and boost a country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP), a downgrade can have devastating effects for an already weak economy. On the other hand, sovereign debts can have important economic effects and it is related, to some degree, to a country's GDP. Consequently, there is a need to study how sovereign credit ratings can moderate the relationship between GDP and sovereign debts. To study sovereign credit rating, Moody's and Standard and Poor's, as two of the most prestigious credit rating agencies, were taken into consideration. Panama's public data from 2000 to 2019 related to GDP and sovereign debt was analyzed. Two moderation analyses were performed to test two hypotheses by using SPSS AMOS Version 27.0. The results in the empirical research demonstrated that sovereign credit rating moderates the relation between the two variables. Moody's and Standard and Poor's sovereign credit rating demonstrated to be significant in both cases.

title: Is it possible to assess the speed of development embedded by any industrial revolution on the society? An analysis under the application of the IRIDS-Index
affiliations: Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School

detail.title: Is it possible to assess the speed of development embedded by any industrial revolution on the society? An analysis under the application of the IRIDS-Index

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE
declarations.ethicsApproval: NONE
declarations.funderStatement: NONE

detail.abstract: The various industrial revolutions that have shaped the modern world provide valuable insights into the potential transformations of both industrialized and non-industrialized societies. This research aims to focus on the seventh industrial revolution, analysing its pros and cons. The study is structured into five parts. In the first section, this paper delves into the evolution of different industrial revolutions, spanning from the first to the fourth, exploring their historical developments in depth (Ward 1994; Russell 2014; Manning 2020). The second section introduces the methodology used to assess these industrial revolutions. The third section involves evaluating the speed of development for each industrial revolution through the introduction of a new model called the "Industrial Revolution Development Speed Index (IRIDS-Index)." This index aims to encapsulate the real impact of each industrial revolution, considering economic, social, technological, and political transformations. The model utilizes both qualitative and quantitative data to assess aspects that have not been evaluated in this manner before. Moving on to the fourth section, this paper calculate and assess our results using the IRIDS-Index to evaluate each industrial revolution based on parameters related to economic, social, political, and technological factors. This comprehensive approach allows for a nuanced understanding of the multifaceted impacts of each revolution. Finally, in the fifth section, this paper presents our conclusions and recommendations derived from the analysis. By examining the seventh industrial revolution through this structured framework, this paper aims to contribute valuable insights into its potential implications across various dimensions of society.

reference: Journal of Law, Economics and Policy, Volume 20, Issue 1 pp. 197-239
title: LPE and the Erasure of the Individual
affiliations: Drake University - Law School

detail.title: LPE and the Erasure of the Individual

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Law, Economics and Policy, Volume 20, Issue 1 pp. 197-239

detail.abstract: The Law and Political Economy (LPE) movement aspires to reshape law to meet modern crises, but in doing so it risks erasing the individual. This article argues that LPE’s analytical and normative frameworks focus so heavily on aggregate outcomes—redistribution, equality, and “democracy as collective power”—that they neglect the incentives, agency, and welfare of individual persons. Through textual analysis of leading LPE scholarship and case studies on crime, climate, and market regulation, the paper shows how LPE’s concepts of coercion, equality, and democracy subvert autonomy and introduce policy pathologies. By contrasting LPE’s macro focus with the micro-analytic insights of law and economics, the article demonstrates how ignoring individual behavior produces counterproductive results, especially for those LPE claims to protect. Reintroducing individual-level analysis, it concludes, is essential for building humane and effective political-economic reform.

reference: UC Davis Legal Studies Research Paper ; Forthcoming (December 2025) Georgetown Immigration Law Journal
title: The Meaning of the End of Chevron for Immigration Removal Adjudications
affiliations: University of California, Davis - School of Law

detail.title: The Meaning of the End of Chevron for Immigration Removal Adjudications

publicationDetails.detailsText: UC Davis Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of California, Davis School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, the Supreme Court in 2024 over the foundational administrative law decision of Chevron, U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. Since 1984, Chevron had required courts to defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous provisions of statutes that they administer. Courts again have the final say on the meaning of the law administered by agencies.

Liberal commentators lament the end of Chevron deference. However, Chevron was no friend to noncitizens. Deference generally meant that courts upheld the U.S. administrative agencies’ interpretation of the immigration statute and agency orders of removal of noncitizens from the United States.

Removal adjudications, which determine whether noncitizens may live in the United States, were not at issue in Chevron, a technical environmental law case involving a pollution emissions rule. Removal adjudications are quite different from the cost/benefit analysis that factors into rules and regulations designed to protect the environment. Through an immigration bureaucracy with the power to remove noncitizens from the United States or gant them relief from removal, such as asylum, attorneys for the U.S. government pursue the removal of noncitizens and attempt to restrict relief from removal provided by the immigration statute passed by Congress. Agencies in the Executive Branch decide those matters. Chevron deference in that bureaucratic landscape for years had adverse consequences for noncitizens, the majority of who are people of color from the developing world.

Even if the Supreme Court’s elimination of Chevron deference does not directly improve matters for noncitizens, independent interpretations of the immigration statute by the courts cannot possibly have more negative impacts than the era of deference did. This Essay evaluates how the Supreme Court’s overruling of Chevron will affect judicial review of agency immigration adjudications and may well benefit noncitizens by allowing the courts to have the final word on the meaning of the law.

title: The Long-Term Wage Effects of Unemployment Rate at Graduation in Japan
affiliations: The University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: The Long-Term Wage Effects of Unemployment Rate at Graduation in Japan
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the long-term effects of labor market entry conditions on earnings in Japan, with a focus on gender disparities and the role of initial employment type at graduation. In the Japanese labor market, men are more likely to enter regular employment, characterized by permanent contracts and strong job security, while women are disproportionately represented in non-regular jobs, such as part-time, temporary, or fixed-term positions, which offer lower wages and fewer benefits. Exploiting temporal and regional variation in the unemployment rate at graduation, I estimate earnings trajectories over the first 20 years of labor market experience. First, I find that a one percentage point increase in the unemployment rate at graduation is associated with a 6.5% decline in contemporaneous earnings for men during the first decade, with the effect fading in the second decade. For women, the estimated effect is smaller (–0.6%) and statistically insignificant. Second, I find that higher unemployment at graduation significantly reduces the likelihood of securing regular employment by 4.7% for men and 3.8% for women. Third, I find that starting one’s career in non-regular employment amplifies wage penalties, with earnings losses of 18.4% for men and 13.6% for women over the first decade, with the wage effects diminishing for men over the second decade. These large penalties are driven by a reduced probability of transitioning into regular employment in subsequent years: 2.1% lower for men and 3.4% lower for women per percentage point increase in the unemployment rate at graduation. Overall, the findings suggest that the costs of entering the labor market during economic downturns are disproportionately borne by workers with less than 10 years of labor market experience, particularly those who begin in non-regular employment. For women who begin their careers in non-regular employment, the long-term consequences appear more persistent.

title: The AI Penalty in Trade Secret Law
affiliations: University of Georgia - C. Herman and Mary Virginia Terry College of Business, University of Miami - Department of Business Law and Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers Law School

detail.title: The AI Penalty in Trade Secret Law

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was approved by the University of Miami Institutional Review Board.

detail.abstract: Factfinders are significantly more likely to assign liability, award higher damages, and judge conduct as improper when defendants use artificial intelligence (AI) systems-rather than humans-to acquire trade secrets, even when the conduct is otherwise identical. This finding, based on original experimental research, reveals that there is an "AI penalty" in trade secret misappropriation cases. In other IP regimes, anti-AI bias is doctrinally inappropriate: the method of infringement should not affect adjudicatory outcomes. But trade secret law is different. Its opentextured standards-such as "improper means," "reasonable measures," and "commercial morality"-demand fact-specific, context-sensitive analyses. As a result, courts may permissibly, even appropriately, reach different conclusions about AI-and human-enabled conduct. Still, when courts penalize AI simply for being AI, they risk codifying a de facto rule that AI and automation are inherently suspect. This is problematic. Normatively, it may chill legitimate uses of AI or incentivize firms to conceal their methods of information gathering. Doctrinally, it undermines the principles behind trade secret law's evolving standards, which must track shifts in technological capabilities and industry adoption. Thus, we outline how courts can articulate clear, principled reasons when treating AI-enabled conduct as improper-preserving the adaptability of trade secret law while ensuring that its evolution remains responsive to, rather than distorted by, new technologies.

title: Covid-19, Social Marginalization, and the Supreme Federal Court of Brazil
affiliations: Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Fundação Getulio Vargas Law School at São Paulo

detail.title: Covid-19, Social Marginalization, and the Supreme Federal Court of Brazil
detail.abstract: This volume has put significant effort into conceptualizing solidarity and analyzing its many dimensions and manifestations. This chapter offers a different approach to understanding solidarity by focusing on its antithesis – social marginalization – and the possibilities of addressing marginalization and its direct consequences via courts. Solidarity designates an idea commonly understood as manifesting itself in the identification with others, in recognising interdependency and mutual obligations between equals, in the joint responsibility and cooperation to realize common goals, and in the effort to approximate, protect and integrate others.2 Marginalization is the negation of solidarity. It is the lack of identification of the community with those perceived as outsiders or belonging to the bottom of society; a diminished sense of empathy, obligation, and responsibility towards them; the refusal to cooperate with them as equals; and an effort to exclude them. Solidarity is a centripetal force that promotes integration, whereas marginalization is a centrifugal force that alienates parts of society.

title: How Interest Rate Cycles Affect Small-Cap IPO Performance: A Quantitative Study of India’s Primary Markets (2018–2024)

detail.title: How Interest Rate Cycles Affect Small-Cap IPO Performance: A Quantitative Study of India’s Primary Markets (2018–2024)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required as this study relies solely on publicly available financial data.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the role of interest rate cycles in the dynamics of small-cap IPOs in India from 2018–2024, a time characterized by changing and volatile interest rates and significant participation of individual investors. Over time, as India’s main markets have matured in size and prominence, small-cap IPOs have become an important barometer of sentiment, speculation, and a liquidity-driven market in India. Loans that are sensitive to macroeconomic factors, primarily to changes in the sensitive to macroeconomic factors, particularly the benchmark repo rate set by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which influences the cost of borrowing and overall investor risk appetite. In this research, I measured the impact of variation in the RBI repo rate on IPOs listing-day returns and, 30 days post listing, performance through correlation analysis and linear regression models on a curated dataset of small-cap IPOs listed at NSE and BSE. These results indicate that the environment of lower interest rates has a systematic impact on the results of IPOs, with higher oversubscription rates and higher short-term returns. In contrast, a market debut is less gung-ho with rate hikes, suggests the bailiffs. This study extends the scant literature on emerging economy IPOs and shows the significance of monetary policy as a fundamental attribution of capital market development. The research provides tactical guidance for investors, policymakers and companies in India on its changing IPO paradigm.

title: Comparative Public Debt of Indian States: Evidence from CAG’s State Finances 2022–23 and RBI Budgets 2024–25
affiliations: Kurukshetra University Kurukshetra

detail.title: Comparative Public Debt of Indian States: Evidence from CAG’s State Finances 2022–23 and RBI Budgets 2024–25
detail.abstract: I compare Indian states' public debt positions and sustainability signals using the Comptroller and Auditor General of India's (CAG) new cross-state State Finances 2022-23 publication and the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) State Finances: A Study of Budgets 2024-25. I benchmark debt-to-GSDP, interest burden, and committed expenditure to map fiscal space. Debt ratios vary widely: several states exceed 35-45% of GSDP, while some large states remain below 20%. Interest-to-revenue ratios above 20% in certain states indicate binding liquidity constraints despite nominal consolidation. Policy priorities include rebuilding primary surpluses through revenue buoyancy, capping subsidy drift, rationalising wage-pension growth, disclosing and fencing contingent liabilities, and smoothing SDL maturity profiles. Results rely on audited 2022-23 data and 2023-24/2024-25 budget estimates; rankings using BE/RE are indicative, not final. (Comptroller and Auditor General of India)

title: Strengthening Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) for Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
affiliations: University of Edenburg, University of Edenburg and University of Edenburg

detail.title: Strengthening Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) for Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
detail.abstract: Establishment of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the year 2015 was a historic global promise of sustainable and inclusive development to the world. Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) is the linchpin that is centrally critical to tracking progress, taking accountabilities, and to enable making of informed decisions that are rooted in rigorous evidence, all for achieving these aspirational goals. The paper puts forth the proposition that attaining the SDGs is inherently precarious and unstable without functioning and robust M&E systems. It not only establishes the primordial importance and centrality of M&E to the sustainable development context but identifies several of the issues and challenges that are inherent to the status quo. It defines specific measures and policies that are intended to strengthen M&E systems so as to achieve wider and deeper effects. Through conceptual analysis, rigorous case studies, and vast statistical evidence, the paper examines the immense ways in which rigorous M&E can enable and allow sustainable progress in the longer term. It champions the call for M&E to transform, to become more inclusive, technology-intelligent, and agile in nature, thereby ensuring that no individual nor populace is left behind in the seminal journey to sustainable development.

title: The Digital Euro as a Governance Tool: Institutional Implications for the European Central Bank?

detail.title: The Digital Euro as a Governance Tool: Institutional Implications for the European Central Bank?
detail.abstract: On 28 June 2023, the European Commission published a legislative proposal for a regulation establishing the Digital Euro-the EU's prospective retail Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC). From a normative perspective, this legislative initiative must both reflect the EU's exclusive competence in monetary policy and, connected to it, remain consistent with the powers conferred on the European Central Bank (ECB) by the Treaties. At the same time, the legal framework of the Digital Euro must be designed in a way not to compromise the constitutional principles of ECB independence and accountability, as captured by the so-called model of "accountable independence." This Article examines how future legislation should be framed to empower the ECB to issue the Digital Euro as a monetary instrument in pursuit of its statutory mandate and tasks, while ensuring an appropriate equilibrium between institutional independence and its accountability obligations. To this end, it focuses on three key legal provisions of the draft Regulation-namely, Articles 15, 16, and 40-examining their implications in light of the existing legal framework governing the European Monetary Union. The Article ultimately proposes targeted amendments to the Digital Euro Regulation to safeguard the constitutional foundations of the single currency and to preserve the European Central Bank's independence and institutional role within the Union.

title: The Womanly Face of Ukraine: The Russian-Ukrainian War through a Gender Lens
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Womanly Face of Ukraine: The Russian-Ukrainian War through a Gender Lens
detail.abstract: The Ukrainian-Russian war is illustrated by media, policy-makers and academia in patriarchal perspectives and definitions: the militaristic paradigm is employed as model in peace processes, the impact of war are analysed through a neutral gender-lens and the offered narration put at the centre the men who left for the front, while overlooking the works and efforts of feminist and women's movements for humanitarian relief and for political and territorial integrity of Ukraine. The study here proposed aims to change this vision related to the Ukrainian-Russian war, by providing a new feminist perspective. The first part highlights how this conflict specifically affects women and their social, political and economic status before the war, while the second part analyses the contribution of women-led NGOs for humanitarian aid and for the implementation of the Women, Peace and Security agenda and the ideological and political position of local and international feminist movement towards the war. In conclusion, a brief excursus on post-conflict plans and on issues regarding the inclusion of a gendermainstreaming approach in peace processes is illustrated through a feminist lens. Literature review is the main analysis approach of this study.

title: From Weather to Wallet: Evidence on Seasonal Temperature Shocks and Global Food Prices
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: From Weather to Wallet: Evidence on Seasonal Temperature Shocks and Global Food Prices
detail.abstract: In this paper, we provide evidence on the impact of global seasonal temperature shocks on global food commodity prices. Utilizing monthly data from 1961 to 2023, we find an economically and statistically highly significant, longer-lasting positive impact of summer temperature shocks on global food commodity prices. In contrast, we do not find such effects for winter, spring or autumn temperature shocks. A summer which is 0.4 °C hotter than in the previous five years, roughly equal to the largest summer shock we observe in our sample, causes food commodity prices to rise by 10% within 12 months. In addition, we show that such weather shocks lower global food production quantities, indicating that such shocks can be classified as supply shocks.

title: Nuclear Deterrence Reconsidered: A Systems Engineering Assessment of Iran's Post-June 2025 Nuclear Options
affiliations: University of Tehran - Faculty of Law and Political Sciences

detail.title: Nuclear Deterrence Reconsidered: A Systems Engineering Assessment of Iran's Post-June 2025 Nuclear Options
detail.abstract: The June 13-24, 2025 counterproliferation campaign against Iranian nuclear infrastructure provides unprecedented empirical data for assessing nuclear deterrence viability under contemporary strategic conditions. This interdisciplinary analysis employs systems engineering methodology, game-theoretic modeling, and multi-criteria decision analysis to evaluate three strategic pathways: nuclear breakout, enhanced latency, and conventional deterrence modernization. Through integration of nuclear engineering principles, detection physics, command-control systems analysis, and strategic studies frameworks, we demonstrate that nuclear weaponization would constitute a net security liability rather than enhancement for Iran. Key findings indicate that contemporary monitoring capabilities, intervention technologies, and regional dynamics have fundamentally altered proliferation cost-benefit calculations, rendering nuclear weapons strategically counterproductive for middle powers under intensive international scrutiny.

title: A Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation of Biases in Expectation Formation
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: A Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation of Biases in Expectation Formation
detail.abstract: We revisit predictability of forecast errors in macroeconomic survey data, which is often taken as evidence against rational expectations. We argue that to reject rational expectations, one must be able to predict forecast errors out of sample. However, the regressions used in the literature often perform poorly out of sample and could not have helped to improve forecasts in real time. We do find notable exceptions, in particular slow adjustment and mean bias in interest rate forecasts and excess dispersion in individual forecasts. Our findings narrow down the set of biases that merit closer attention of researchers in behavioral macroeconomics.

title: Multi-party issuance of stablecoins and other types of crypto-assets
affiliations: Universite du Luxembourg - Faculty of Law, Economics and Finance

detail.title: Multi-party issuance of stablecoins and other types of crypto-assets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a member of the Task Force on Crypto-assets and Decentralised Finance (CATF) of the European Systemic Risk Board. The views laid out herein are purely the authors’ personal view and unrelated to the works of the ESRB.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Luxembourg Research Fund (FNR), grant NCER22/IS/16570468/NCER-FT.

detail.abstract:
Technical, market, and regulatory fragmentation drive cooperation in decentralised finance globally. This paper examines which types of cooperation are permissible under the Markets in Crypto-assets Regulation (MiCA), focusing on the multi-party issuance of stablecoins and other crypto-assets. It identifies the parallel issuance and syndicate models as legally accepted archetypes of crypto cooperation under MiCA and analyses the corresponding regulatory requirements.

The discussion addresses the need for a policy response to multi-issuer crypto schemes. Token holder protection calls for detailed disclosures on the participating parties and their accountability. For e-money tokens (EMTs) and asset-referenced tokens (ARTs), an appropriate organisational structure for cooperation should be ensured. Systemic risk concerns warrant a close look at reserve handling and outsourced relationships with technical service providers and developer firms. However, an objective-based interpretation of Article 34 MiCA, Article 19(6) Payment Services Directive, and the application of the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) provide the means to mitigate such risks. Looking ahead, the integration of important crypto infrastructure providers in the Eurosystem framework for financial market infrastructure, as well as the introduction of a substituted compliance/equivalence framework into MiCA, would further strengthen regulatory coherence.

title: Creationomics
affiliations: Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School

detail.title: Creationomics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE
declarations.ethicsApproval: NONE
declarations.funderStatement: NONE

detail.abstract: This paper presents a new field in economics is called "Creationomics." Creationomics proposes a systematic study of how creative thinking can generate, transform, and apply economic knowledge. It views creativity not merely as a contributor to innovation in markets, but as an analytical force that reshapes the construction of models, the design of policy, and the architecture of institutions. This paper defines the foundations of the field, identifies its principal domains model design, policy innovation, institutional development, pedagogy, and interdisciplinary integration and outlines key research questions. By embedding artistic, design, and scientific creativity into economic reasoning, Creationomics offers tools for understanding complex behaviours and crafting adaptive responses to persistent challenges such as inequality, sustainability, and technological disruption. The article argues that recognising creativity as an intrinsic component of economic analysis can expand both the scope and the practical relevance of the discipline.

title: Southeast Asia's Stalled Development: Semi-Peripheral Growth, Elite Entrenchment and Geopolitical Dynamics

detail.title: Southeast Asia's Stalled Development: Semi-Peripheral Growth, Elite Entrenchment and Geopolitical Dynamics
detail.abstract: This article examines Southeast Asia's trajectory from Cold War developmental success to contemporary stagnation. Drawing on a critical political economy approach that synthesises the Murdoch school of Southeast Asian studies with world-systems theory and international relations scholarship, the analysis situates the region's predicament within the framework of semi-peripheral development. This denotes a condition where states occupy intermediate positions in global hierarchies that constrain developmental options while generating distinctive patterns of political and geopolitical adaptation. The study examines cases across Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand to reveal how semi-peripheral positioning produces not only economic dependencies and illiberal hybrid political systems but also distinctive geopolitical behaviour characterised by multidirectional foreign policies and strategic hedging. Far from representing policy failure, these patterns reflect a stable structural condition of "constrained sovereignty" where formal independence coexists with tight boundaries imposed by global market integration and elite capture. These findings suggest that traditional approaches to development studies and international relations require reconceptualisation toward integrated analysis of how material structures, class relations, and interstate competition mutually constitute one another. To this end, the paper advances an approach grounded in cross-disciplinary exploration at the intersection of development studies, political economy, and international relations, aiming to move beyond outdated development orthodoxies. Through this lens, Southeast Asia's experience illuminates a broader transformation from developmental showcase to semi-peripheral predicament. This shift reflects the exhaustion of universalist development paradigms and the emergence of more fragmented, competitive approaches to global economic transformation.

title: Soft Artificial  Intelligence (SAI) and Hard Artificial Intelligence (HAI)
affiliations: Universiti Kuala Lumpur Business School

detail.title: Soft Artificial  Intelligence (SAI) and Hard Artificial Intelligence (HAI)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a new perspective on artificial intelligence (AI) and proposes a new division of it. The study is organized into two main sections: soft artificial intelligence (SAI) and hard artificial intelligence (HAI). It also presents a new definition of AI within this framework. In addition, the paper examines the impact of AI on the future of the market structure, highlighting its role in reshaping the production function and relocating its factors of production: labour, land, capital, and entrepreneur. These changes are expected to drive a profound reorganization of both the economy and society over the future. To address these challenges, we propose a basic economic theoretical framework that can provide a clearer understanding of the future of our increasingly complex and dynamic economic world.
